e4144441f5e43a65: JERUSALEM: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu boasted of his endorsement from Donald Trump on the eve of Israel's election, suggesting the two leaders could restart their war against Iran if he wins, after Trump said they should "finish the job".
"US president Donald Trump has come with a friendship that has never existed before between an Israeli prime minister and an American president.
"And it is doubtful we will ever have such a friendly president again," Netanyahu said in a televised appearance late on Sunday night.
"He has another two years, and he says he is calling on you to vote for me," he added.

In his own social media post on Sunday, Trump, who launched the Iran war jointly with Netanyahu in February, said: "Vote for Bibi Netanyahu for Prime Minister, we have to finish the job that we started!"
Netanyahu said Trump was willing to take action "that would finally, finally, remove the Iranian threat", but only as long as Netanyahu himself remains in power.

"And I have already instructed the Mossad and the IDF (military) to bring down this regime, to bring down this regime because that is the only way to put an end to this threat," Netanyahu said, referring to Israel's main intelligence service and military.

Asked for comment on Netanyahu's remarks, White House deputy press secretary Anna Kelly said: “As president Trump stated, Iran is in very bad condition, both economically and militarily, and the blockade will remain in full force and effect, with oil flowing in record numbers of barrels through the Hormuz Strait."
"The US will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the midterm elections," Kelly added via email, referring to the Nov 3 vote in the US.
Netanyahu's leading opponent, centrist former military chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot, posted his own comments on social media, praising Trump as "a true friend of Israel".
"I value his efforts and his commitment to Israel’s security, and I am confident that he will work in full cooperation with any leader chosen by the people," he said.
Eisenkot accuses Netanyahu of fear-mongering

Tuesday's vote, Israel's first since the Oct 7, 2023, Hamas attacks, is the first chance for voters to deliver a verdict on the worst security failure in generations and the wars on multiple fronts that followed.
With Netanyahu already at the helm of the most right-wing government in Israeli history, politics have shifted even further to the right.
Nearly all Jewish-led parties, including that of the hawkish Eisenkot, now oppose the "two-state solution" that underpinned decades of peace negotiations with the Palestinians.
However, many voters say the divisive politics of Israel's longest-serving leader make the country weaker.
Polls suggest Netanyahu's Likud Party will lose seats, potentially depriving his coalition of right-wing, far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties of its narrow majority.
Eisenkot and an array of opposition parties ranging from the rump of the centre-left to the right, also have no clear path to unseat him.

Netanyahu, 77, is an unrivaled master of political survival: the only time since 2009 that opponents managed to wrest him briefly from the premiership, it took four inconclusive elections within two years to get him out. He was back 18 months later.

Neither side planned major public events for Monday. But both posted on social media, drumming on the election's major themes — for Netanyahu, that he is the only leader with the mettle to face down Israel's enemies; for his opponents, that his divisive politics have weakened the country.

Netanyahu shared an AI-generated video on Monday of Iran's supreme leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, whose father Ali Khamenei was killed on the first night of US-Israeli strikes on Iran in February. Lying in a hospital bed, the younger Khamenei says his own vote would be "definitely not Bibi. Another term like this and I will be meeting my father sooner than expected".
On Sunday, Netanyahu posted a computer-generated photo of a mushroom cloud over Tel Aviv, saying Israel was in existential danger from Iran.
Eisenkot responded by accusing him of "relying on a campaign of fear-mongering, lies, and threats—including images of nuclear bombs in the heart of Tel Aviv. This time, it won’t work for him".
Trump's endorsement of Netanyahu carries its own political risks a week before a legislative election in which his own Republicans are seeking to hold onto power.
The Iran war is deeply unpopular in the US, blamed for a surge in prices, especially for fuel.
Major fighting has been suspended for months after ceasefire negotiations held without Israeli participation.

2317660be2420d01: KUALA LUMPUR: Pembangunan Bandar Madani Bukit Jalil akan dilaksanakan secara berfasa dalam tempoh 15 tahun, dengan kerajaan dalam proses menyediakan peruntukan RM250 juta bagi menaik taraf jalan raya dan mengurangkan kesesakan trafik di kawasan itu.

Menteri Perumahan dan Kerajaan Tempatan Nga Kor Ming berkata, peruntukan itu akan digunakan untuk kerja menaik taraf jalan sedia ada, membina jalan baharu empat lorong serta dua jambatan bagi melancarkan aliran trafik, sekali gus menangani kebimbangan penduduk setempat.

Pembangunan itu, katanya, bukan sekadar projek perumahan berkepadatan tinggi, sebaliknya sebuah ekosistem bandar berintegrasi yang menggabungkan kediaman mampu milik dengan kemudahan pendidikan, kesihatan dan komuniti.

“Projek ini direka khas untuk memastikan rakyat tidak hanya memiliki kediaman, tetapi menikmati kualiti hidup yang lengkap,” katanya ketika menggulung perbahasan Belanjawan 2027 peringkat dasar bagi Kementerian Perumahan dan Kerajaan Tempatan (KPKT) di Dewan Rakyat hari ini.

Nga berkata, antara komponen utama projek itu ialah pembinaan sekolah secara menegak yang mengintegrasikan prasekolah, sekolah rendah dan sekolah menengah dalam satu kompleks, selain klinik kesihatan moden serta Hab Madani.
Hab Madani itu dicadangkan merangkumi ruang penjaja, kios polis, dewan serba guna, ruang perkhidmatan komuniti, surau, kemudahan pengangkutan dan hentian bas setempat.

Beliau berkata, pembangunan itu turut menerapkan konsep bandar mesra pejalan kaki dalam lingkungan 15 minit (15-Minute Walkable City), dengan kemudahan asas dan kawasan rekreasi dihubungkan melalui laluan pejalan kaki berbumbung bagi mengurangkan kebergantungan kepada kenderaan persendirian untuk perjalanan jarak dekat.

Mengenai kebimbangan terhadap kesan pembangunan kepada penduduk sedia ada, Nga berkata Penilaian Impak Trafik, Penilaian Impak Alam Sekitar dan Penilaian Impak Sosial sedang dilaksanakan secara teliti.

Beliau berkata, projek itu telah memperoleh Perintah Pembangunan daripada Dewan Bandaraya Kuala Lumpur (DBKL) selepas melalui proses libat urus teknikal bersama agensi berkaitan, termasuk PLANMalaysia, Kementerian Kesihatan, Kementerian Pendidikan, Jabatan Kerja Raya dan Majlis Bandaraya Subang Jaya.

Menjawab celahan Dr Zaliha Mustafa (PH-Sekijang) mengenai rasional pemilihan Bukit Jalil sebagai lokasi projek itu, Nga berkata, kawasan itu dipilih kerana kedudukannya yang strategik serta mempunyai jaringan perhubungan yang baik dengan prasarana awam.
Beliau berkata, kediaman yang ditawarkan juga akan berada pada kadar mampu milik, berbanding harga kondominium di kawasan bandar raya yang boleh mencecah RM600,000 hingga RM700,000.

Sebelum ini, Ahli Parlimen Seputeh Teresa Kok menggesa kerajaan menangguhkan pendaftaran Rumah Madani di Bandar Madani Bukit Jalil sehingga kajian pelan kawalan mikro Bukit Jalil dan Pelan Tempatan Kuala Lumpur 2040 (PTKL 2040) selesai berikutan kebimbangan pembangunan akan memburukkan kesesakan trafik.

Dalam pada itu, Nga dalam kenyataan memaklumkan, sebanyak RM467,140 kutipan denda direkodkan, manakala 3,638 jam hukuman khidmat masyarakat dikenakan terhadap individu yang disabitkan kesalahan membuang sampah kecil di tempat awam bagi tempoh Januari hingga September tahun ini.

Katanya, perkara itu hasil daripada 8,960 operasi penguatkuasaan dilaksanakan di tujuh negeri di bawah Akta Pengurusan Sisa Pepejal dan Pembersihan Awam 2007, dengan 17,145 Notis Pemberitahuan Kesalahan telah dikeluarkan.

Nga berkata, KPKT akan terus mempergiat operasi penguatkuasaan sempena Tahun Melawat Malaysia 2026 dan 2027 bagi memastikan persekitaran negara kekal bersih serta memberikan imej positif kepada pelancong.
“Seiring dengan usaha tersebut, KPKT turut menggerakkan penyertaan masyarakat melalui Hari Cuci Malaysia (HCM) bagi meningkatkan kesedaran awam terhadap kepentingan kebersihan awam.

“Penganjuran HCM tahun ini mencatatkan dua rekod Malaysia Book of Records, iaitu bagi Penyertaan Gotong-Royong Teramai dalam Sehari, melibatkan 332,429 peserta dan Pengumpulan Sisa Kitar Semula Terberat dalam Sehari, berjumlah 89,221.22kg,” katanya.
424b22ba2a898685: AUSTIN, Texas—Formula 1 returned to US shores this weekend with its annual visit to the Circuit of the Americas in Austin, Texas. Once in danger of falling off the calendar due to a lack of interest, it’s now one of the most popular tracks on the calendar and, of the US’s three races, it's the one the real fans mostly attend.

Unlike Miami or Las Vegas, which race on temporary street circuits, COTA is a permanent race track with plenty of run-off areas instead of concrete walls. Designed by motorcycle racer Kevin Schwanz—Herman Tilke’s company did only the buildings and infrastructure, contrary to popular belief—the track combines a mix of corner speeds with challenging turn sequences, a few heavy braking zones, and plenty of elevation changes.

It’s a place Ars knows rather intimately by now. We’ve driven it in everything from an Audi TT-S to a Corvette ZR1 to a bicycle, and that’s just in the real world. Over the years, we’ve been there for F1 to learn about how the sport puts together its broadcasts, how Pirelli designs its tires, and how various tech partners help teams manage their data and strategies. We even saw the race through a neophyte’s eyes. And that’s just F1—we’ve logged many hours there with the World Endurance Championship and IMSA for the Lone Star Le Mans races in sweaty September.
8c2dedaa19c1a2ec: NASA's Swift observatory made its final observation on October 20 and is expected to re-enter the atmosphere in the next few weeks after a failed rescue attempt over the summer.

Designed to study gamma-ray bursts, Swift was launched on November 20, 2004, on a two-year mission. It has lasted almost 22 years, but atmospheric drag is inexorably lowering the spacecraft's orbit, so reentry is likely just shy of the vehicle's 22nd anniversary. Swift has no propulsion system to save itself.
Swift is now orbiting at an altitude of less than 171 miles above Earth's surface, meaning it cannot keep its telescopes steady when pointing at astronomical targets.

Because the spacecraft could no longer compensate for the increased drag, it dropped into safe mode. A command was then sent from the ground that, according to NASA, "effectively ended Swift operations to prepare it for re-entry."

The descent of Swift has accelerated in recent years due to increased solar activity. Last year, NASA awarded Katalyst Space a contract for a high-risk, high-reward mission to boost the observatory to a higher orbit. Swift's science operations were curtailed to maximize opportunities for Katalyst Space's LINK spacecraft, but alas, a rendezvous never happened, and engineers opted to reactivate operations to eke out as much science as possible.
The expected side effect was increased drag on the spacecraft and, as expected, Swift sank rapidly until operations had to cease.

Swift has been an astonishingly productive instrument during its long life. According to NASA, it has observed more than 2,000 gamma-ray bursts and more than 1,400 supernova explosions. It has conducted an all-sky X-ray survey and seen stars shredded by black holes.
The full Swift archive comes to approximately 12 terabytes. Not too bad for something that was only supposed to last two years.

NASA now faces the problem that it has no direct replacement for Swift. As well as paying tribute to the observatory's contributions, Shawn Domagal-Goldman, director of the Astrophysics Division at NASA Headquarters in Washington, said in a statement:

"To support rapid response to cosmic events in a post-Swift world, we're exploring our ability to use and augment NASA's fleet of existing space telescopes, from fast-to-orbit commercial capabilities to efficient, innovative new missions." ®

38d696ce9d9b8a79: GENEVA: Israel has committed the crime against humanity of "extermination" in the West Bank, while continuing to commit "genocide" against Palestinians in the Gaza Strip, United Nations-mandated investigators said Monday.
The UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry said Israeli forces had also committed other crimes against humanity and war crimes in the West Bank, which Israel has occupied since 1967.

The commission, which does not speak for the UN itself, first determined in a September 2025 report that Israel had committed "genocide" in the war in Gaza following Hamas' deadly October 7, 2023 attack on Israel - a finding Israel flatly rejects.

In a new report – which comes the day before Israel's general election – the investigation found that in the West Bank, through military operations reinforced by sustained settler violence, Israel has waged a "widespread and systematic attack" against civilians.

"The Israeli authorities and forces have committed the crimes against humanity of extermination, torture, rape and other forms of sexual violence in the West Bank, as well as persecution based on intersecting discriminatory grounds, with nationality, race and ethnicity at its core," it said.
Israel's mission in Geneva said the report was part of the inquiry's "misinformation campaign to demonise the State of Israel and portray its very existence as criminal."
"The international community must reject these distortions, repudiate the commission's findings and demand its immediate dissolution," it said in a statement.
The three-member investigative team was established by the UN Human Rights Council in 2021.
South African former High Court judge Navi Pillay, who chaired the investigation until November 2025, won the Nobel Peace Prize earlier this month.
The commission's new report focused on killings and bodily and mental harm caused by both Israeli and Palestinian security forces since October 2023.
It found that the situation in the West Bank has deteriorated gravely since the Palestinian Islamist group Hamas's attack from Gaza that month.
The commission found that the Israeli authorities "intended to collectively punish" West Bank civilians due to the Hamas attack.
"The targeting of Palestinian civilians across different locations in the West Bank indicates a high level of coordination and organised planning and is the product of state policy," the report said.
The conduct of Israeli authorities indicates that "they knew and intended settler violence" to be part of the widespread and systematic attack in the West Bank, it added.

"The intentional killing and injuring of Palestinian civilians and destruction of homes in the West Bank combined with Israel's persistent denial of responsibility form part of a broader strategy to exterminate and displace Palestinians and impose conditions of life that are unliveable," said commission chairman Srinivasan Muralidhar.

"Attempting to equate Palestinian statehood with a threat to the existence of Israel is blocking any viable attempts to realise Palestinians' right to self-determination," the Indian judge said in a statement.
The report cited cases where the commission concluded that Israeli forces intended to seriously harm and kill civilians, in acts which amount to war crimes including wilful killing.
The Hamas attack in October 2023 resulted in the deaths of 1,221 people, according to an AFP tally based on official Israeli figures.

Israel's military offensive, in response, has displaced nearly the entire population of Gaza and killed more than 74,200 people, according to Gaza's health ministry, which is under Hamas authority but whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.

"The cases investigated for this report show that the Israeli authorities and forces continue to commit genocidal acts with the genocidal intent to destroy, in whole or in part, the Palestinians in Gaza," the report said.
The inquiry urged Israel to "end the commission of genocide in Gaza" and act immediately on "obligations to prevent and punish genocide and incitement to genocide."
Israel should "immediately end the unlawful occupation of Palestinian territory", and remove all settlers and settlements.

Turning to the Palestinian Authority, the report said that "Palestinian state violence has targeted and continues to target members of opposing Palestinian armed groups and repress Palestinian civil and political opposition."
The Palestinian Authority struggles with credibility and legitimacy, and "targets Palestinians who voice dissenting civil and political views... resulting in killings", it said.
"The Palestinian Authority has also failed to conduct prompt, effective and impartial investigations into incidents of killings."
There was no immediate reaction from the Palestinian Authority.
The commission is due to present its report to the UN General Assembly in New York on Monday.

b0be826e4c1b5fc3: PETALING JAYA: The government has set a 12-month timeline to complete four key studies before deciding Malaysia’s nuclear energy pathway, says science, technology and innovation minister Chang Lih Kang.
Chang said the studies were being carried out under the nuclear energy technology development programme overseen by the energy transition and water transformation ministry.
The studies would cover the owner-operator model and financing plan, site assessment and prioritisation, technology assessment, and the pathway for developing Malaysia’s nuclear industry, he said.
“These studies will be completed within 12 months," he said when winding up the 2027 budget debate for his ministry in the Dewan Rakyat today.
“After that, the government will decide whether to use floating small modular reactors (SMRs) or land-based SMRs, and which model should be adopted."

This comes amid calls from MPs on both sides for Malaysia to accelerate its preparations for a more uncertain energy future, with rising electricity demand from artificial intelligence and data centres, geopolitical tensions, and continued reliance on oil and gas.

Howard Lee (PH-Ipoh Timur) urged the government to accelerate its preparations, saying Malaysia could not afford to wait until a final decision on nuclear energy before beginning work on the technology.
Lee argued that the country needed to consider interim options given rising energy prices amid tensions in West Asia and growing electricity demand from data centres, particularly in Johor.
Even if Malaysia decided to proceed with a floating SMR after the studies, he said, obtaining equipment, assembling components and constructing the facility could still take around five years.
Lee also said that Malaysia may already have much of the regulatory groundwork in place.
“If I am not mistaken, the mapping of legislation, laws and regulations is already about 80% to 90% in place (for floating SMRs),” he said, adding that only a smaller portion remained unclear.
Wan Ahmad Fayhsal Wan Ahmad Kamal (PN-Machang) had made a similar argument in the Dewan Rakyat, calling for Malaysia to accelerate its nuclear planning as it confronts broader energy-security risks.
He pointed to the crisis around the Strait of Hormuz, and warned that oil and gas would remain a major challenge for the economy.
“It is time for Malaysia to take serious and consistent steps to develop our first nuclear power plant,” he said, adding that the project would require “brave decisions” from the government.
SMRs among options
In his winding-up speech, Chang said floating SMRs were among the options being assessed, but no decision had been made on the technology.
“There are land-based SMRs, floating SMRs and others. We will take into account suitability, needs and the country’s circumstances,” he said.
He was responding to Lee, who asked whether the energy transition and water transformation ministry, and the science, technology and innovation ministry were prepared to consider floating SMRs.
Public acceptance crucial
Chang also said the parliamentary debate showed that MPs recognised the need to explore nuclear energy as an alternative source of power.
“For MPs, we see there is a need to explore nuclear energy as one of the alternatives,” he said.
Khairil Nizam Khirudin (PN-Jerantut) also called for Malaysia to explore nuclear energy, saying the technology was neither new nor untested.
However, he said that nuclear energy remained a sensitive issue in Malaysia because of concerns over past nuclear incidents, such as the2011 Fukushima nuclear disaster in Japan.
He called for greater public education and engagement, including among school and university students and MPs who may eventually scrutinise nuclear legislation.
In response, Chang said that public acceptance would remain crucial to any decision to pursue nuclear energy, adding that Mosti was working to make the subject less taboo.
“If the public does not accept the government’s proposal, a (nuclear) project like this will be difficult to continue," he said.

As such, Chang said the ministry has introduced nuclear advocacy as a new element of National Science Week 2026, with public engagement focusing on scientific facts, safety concerns and radioactive-waste management.
2b08e320fe4f0a4e: BERLIN: Germany's Chancellor Friedrich Merz left Monday for visits to Singapore, Japan and South Korea this week while president Frank-Walter Steinmeier heads to China.
Europe's top economy has been seeking to diversify its strategic and trade links in light of the US becoming a less reliable ally and China's growth as an economic rival.
"Merz's Asia trip shows Berlin is "very systematically and strategically expanding its partnership with the nations of the Indo-Pacific," said a government source.
The chancellor, joined by a large business delegation, was due to meet Singapore's prime minister Lawrence Wong on Tuesday and Japan's prime minister Sanae Takaichi on Wednesday.
On Thursday the German leader meets South Korea's president Lee Jae Myung, and on Friday he is to visit the Demilitarised Zone (DMZ) separating North and South Korea.
Steinmeier, the head of state, will deliver a speech at Peking University on Thursday and the following day meet Chinese president Xi Jinping and Premier Li Qiang.
"The focus of the president's trip is on the diverse and complex relations between Germany and China as well as the challenges they present," his office said in a statement.
China is Germany's top economic partner in Asia and has long been a major investment destination, but is also seen as a growing competitor and systemic rival with close ties to Russia.
Germany views the democracies of Japan and South Korea and the business-friendly city-state of Singapore as like-minded partners, according to experts.
cae4e46ce71cfd91: PETALING JAYA: The government is in the process of allocating RM250 million to upgrade roads and build two bridges around the Bukit Jalil Bandar Madani project, which will be developed in phases over 15 years.

Nga said the residential units offered will be priced affordably, in contrast to other condominiums in the city, which can reach between RM600,000 and RM700,000.

212464e5f001c380: SEPANG: Lufthansa has returned to Kuala Lumpur after nearly a decade, restoring nonstop flights to Frankfurt with plans to increase the service to daily from the summer 2027 schedule.
The German carrier operates five flights a week using a 287-seat Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner equipped with its Allegris cabin, offering business, premium economy and economy classes.

Lufthansa Group senior vice president global sales Frank Naeve said the service reconnects two important cities and regions, creating opportunities for business and trade between Malaysia, Germany and Europe.
"With this new service, we are once again connecting two important cities and regions directly with each other."

"But a new route is much more than just connecting two points on a map. It very much follows the purpose of the Lufthansa Group, which is to connect people, cultures, and economies in a sustainable way," he said at Lufthansa's inaugural flight's arrival at Kuala Lumpur International Airport (KLIA) Terminal 1 today.
Naeve said Lufthansa will increase the frequency to daily flights starting next year's summer schedule.
"Initially, we have five services per week, but already today we have announced that we will operate daily services from the summer schedule 2027.
"So that very much reflects our commitment to this market and to connecting the two countries," he said.
He added that the route also strengthens Malaysia's air freight connectivity through Lufthansa Cargo, supporting trade flows between Europe, Malaysia and Southeast Asia.
"Let me also say one additional thing, the cargo contribution to these passenger services is extremely important in order to secure the economics.
"So that's why we're looking forward to a strong commitment also here in Kuala Lumpur for the cargo that we transport on these flights," he said.
Malaysia Airports Holdings Bhd (MAHB) managing director Datuk Mohd Izani Ghani said Lufthansa's return follows sustained collaboration between the airport operator and the airline.
He said the direct connection carries economic significance for Malaysia.
"Germany is Malaysia's largest trading partner in the European Union, with extensive investments across various industries," he said.
Mohd Izani said the route also supports high-value exports by linking Malaysia's manufacturing hubs with Europe.
"This milestone represents close alignment across our government and industry," he said.
According to MAHB, Lufthansa's return brings KLIA's direct European network to five destinations served by five airlines.
KLIA handled 1.1 million passengers on European routes in the first nine months of 2026, up 29.7 per cent year-on-year.

German ambassador to Malaysia Silke Riecken-Daerr said the connection serves businesses seeking opportunities in both markets, as well as students, researchers, tourists and families travelling between the two countries.
She said Lufthansa's decision to return is a vote of confidence in Malaysia and gives fresh momentum to bilateral ties.

Deputy Tourism, Arts and Culture Minister Chiew Choon Man said Malaysia recorded 1.18 million visitors from Europe between January and August 2026, an increase of 1.2 per cent from 1.16 million in the same period last year.
Germany accounted for 116,824 visitors during the eight-month period.
Chiew, who represented Tourism, Arts and Culture Minister Datuk Seri Tiong King Sing at the event, said reliable air connectivity is central to Malaysia's efforts to attract international visitors.

"Strong and reliable air connectivity is fundamental to our efforts to attract more international visitors and ensure that Malaysia remains accessible and competitive in the global tourism market," he said.
He said Malaysia aims to strengthen its presence in the European market, encourage longer stays and create more opportunities for the tourism industry.

e943d9d048be0082: KUALA LUMPUR: Malaysia remains committed to providing RM100 million in reconstruction aid to Gaza, as announced by Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim last year, but its implementation has been hampered by the deteriorating security situation in the territory.

Mohamad said that the Foreign Ministry, through the Malaysian Embassy in Kathmandu, had raised the matter with Nepal's Ministry of Foreign Affairs via a diplomatic note on May 24, 2023, while a meeting with the Nepal Tourism Department was also held on July 7 this year, to seek consideration for the issuance of a death declaration for the climber.
He said that the ministry would continue discussions with the Nepalese authorities, and assist the family in obtaining legal services to apply for a court order on the matter.

On the West Asia crisis, he said that Malaysia continued to diversify its sources of supply, including crude oil and fertilisers, to reduce dependence on a single source, amid geopolitical tensions which had disrupted global supply chains.
Mohamad said the crisis had taught Malaysia the importance of having alternative sources to ensure that supplies of essential goods remained uninterrupted during conflicts.
Malaysia was also exploring opportunities to source phosphate from Algeria and Jordan, which could potentially work with local companies to produce the material for the fertiliser industry, he said.

a42aa930488e6279: KUALA LUMPUR: Indonesian environmental non-governmental organisation Wahana Lingkungan Hidup Indonesia (WALHI) has claimed that 21 companies linked to business groups with Malaysian ties were involved in forest and land fires in Indonesia between January and September 2026.
The findings are part of a mapping analysis report titled "Who Are Behind the Fires?" released by WALHI's National Executive.

According to the report, satellite data recorded at least 30,927 hotspots across Indonesia in the first nine months of this year, with nearly 50 per cent located within the operating concessions of oil palm plantation and forestry companies.

The regions with the highest concentrations of hotspots included West Kalimantan, with 9,529, and Central Kalimantan, with 7,141. The fires caused the Air Pollution Standard Index (ISPU) in affected areas to reach unhealthy to hazardous levels.

The analysis also found that at least 21 concession-holding companies in Indonesia with detected hotspots or fire incidents were subsidiaries of, or affiliated with, business groups originating from Malaysia.

Apart from Malaysian-linked companies, the WALHI report revealed that many other high-risk concessions were controlled by foreign capital and conglomerates with parent entities or registered shareholders in Singapore, Hong Kong and tax havens such as the British Virgin Islands and Samoa.

Meanwhile, on Oct 5, Greenpeace Indonesia and Pantau Gambut alleged that plantation companies from Malaysia and Singapore were among 20 entities linked to forest fires, based on a dataset of haze sources covering Aug 1 to Oct 1.
The report said some of the same Indonesian entities had also been identified in a 2019 report in connection with fires on land they owned.
WALHI said forest and land fires in Indonesia should not be viewed merely as technical errors or negligence by local companies holding permits.
Instead, it said the problem was structural, involving parent business groups that controlled operational policies and benefited economically from their control of the land.

The NGO called on the authorities and relevant ministries to take firm action, including reviewing permits, imposing administrative restrictions, suspending operations and revoking concession permits held by companies that repeatedly experienced fires in areas under their control.

It said the recurring pattern of hotspots across subsidiaries belonging to the same business groups showed that the fires were not isolated incidents caused by negligence among individuals on the ground.

Unity government spokesman Datuk Seri Fahmi Fadzil, on Oct 16, had said that no Malaysian plantation companies with oil palm concessions in Indonesia had been found to be involved in forest fires linked to the haze.
He said cross-checks with Malaysian companies showed that most of the fires observed had occurred outside concessions owned by Malaysian firms.
ff648790db356a0a: KUANTAN: Astro Awani senior journalist Mohd Zailani Md Atan, who was based in Pahang, died at his home here today.

b784b1a0f4ba5ddb: ADDIS ABABA: More than 40 people were killed in an attack on Orthodox Christian churches and homes in Ethiopia's central state of Oromia on Saturday, residents and a conflict monitor told AFP on Monday.

Oromia, Ethiopia's largest state with some 40 million people, has faced a long-running insurgency and ethnic tensions between its Muslim, Protestant and Orthodox communities, which have been increasingly exploited by armed groups.

Local residents and the ACLED conflict monitor told AFP that at least 43 people were killed and 18 wounded when an unidentified armed group attacked villages in the Shirka district of Oromia, around 270km south of the capital, Addis Ababa.

"The attack is said to be religiously motivated and to have targeted Orthodox Christians," ACLED said, adding that the attack led to clashes with local militias and lasted through Saturday afternoon and evening.
Verifying information in Ethiopia is highly challenging due to heavy restrictions on media access. The state-run Ethiopia Human Rights Commission said only that it was "following the situation".
"My sister and uncle were killed, and several of my relatives were taken hostage in Chole ward of Shirka district," one resident told AFP by phone, asking to remain anonymous.
They said 44 people were killed in the region, while another resident put the toll at 51.
ACLED has recorded increasing attacks against Orthodox Christians in the region, starting in February 2023 and escalating since last year.
Ethiopia is a deeply fragmented nation in the Horn of Africa, facing multiple internal conflicts, including heavy fighting that broke out last month in its northern Tigray state.
It was not clear if the attacks involved the primary insurgent group operating in the state, the Oromo Liberation Front.
While concerns over political and ethnic representation have been the main drivers of the insurgency, religion has been used to mobilise fighters.
"We are deeply shocked by these tragic killings and are appealing to the government to intervene and restore security," said a deacon of one of the attacked churches, who put the death toll at 46.
"Some locals have taken refuge in nearby churches," he added.

69904ff11434ac2a: Today, I’m talking to Kevin Roose, journalist and author of the new book The AGI Chronicles, which details the recent and explosive transformation of the AI industry.

Kevin was a longtime New York Times reporter and host of the popular podcast Hard Fork, but he and friend of the show Casey Newton just left the Times to start the all-new tech podcast Machine Gods, which launched last week.

Kevin and I talked about launching Machine Gods and what it’s like to go from The New York Times to being an independent creator — and then of course we talked about the book, which is an excellently reported dive into the companies racing to build artificial general intelligence.

I wanted to get a sense from Kevin of what it was like to report this, to try and understand these characters and this moment in time, and where it all goes next. Fair warning: This conversation takes a pretty philosophical turn at the end, but I think you’ll find it a really worthwhile back-and-forth.
Okay: Kevin Roose on The AGI Chronicles, starting Machine Gods, and where AI goes from here. Here we go.
This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.
Kevin Roose, you are the author of The AGI Chronicles and the cofounder and co-host of the new podcast Machine Gods. Welcome to Decoder.
Thanks so much for having me.
I was listening to the first episode of Machine Gods and you and Casey discussed the fact that technically you have the title of CEO.

It’s true. I won the coin flip and we needed someone. When you start a company as we have, you need to list someone as the CEO, I guess, to know who to haul in front of Congress when our first scandal inevitably breaks. So that’s going to be me.
It’s funny because you’re a CEO on Decoder. It means I’m going to have to ask you the Decoder questions.
[Laughs] Okay. Well, I’ve been a CEO for about five minutes and most days I frankly forget I’m the CEO.
Honestly, that tracks with most of the CEOs on the show. They all act like they’ve only done it for five minutes. We’ll come to it.

I want to talk about your book. It’s called The AGI Chronicles. It is a meticulously reported book about the main frontier labs and the culture shift they’ve all undergone as AI has come into the forefront and become a much more commercial product in many ways.

But let’s just start with Machine Gods. You were a journalist for The New York Times for a long time. Obviously, I think the audience probably knows this, but you and I have known each other for a long time. I will say that since I have known you, your desire to be a YouTuber has been top of mind. You’re just like, “How do I get over there?” And I’ve always been like, “Run, don’t do it.” But you did it.

You left The Times, you started your own podcast with our friend Casey Newton. It is the next generation of the very popular podcast, Hard Fork, which was excellent. And I’m excited for you, but what made you take the leap?
Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here. Not a subscriber? You can sign up here.
Yeah, you have been trying to convince me out of this for as long as I’ve been trying to convince myself into it and you have not succeeded because here I am.
Yep, I failed. Utterly failed.

No, look, I think that for some very good reasons, media companies have long been a little bit wary of going all in on YouTube or any other video platform. The ones that have gone all in have not necessarily come out of that with good feelings about it because there are a lot of–
Yeah, they pivot to video and also into death, routinely.

Yeah, you pivot to video or you sort of waste a bunch of money doing things that don’t pay for themselves. So, I think there are some structural economic reasons for that, but I also think it’s that there aren’t a lot of institutions that are equipped to make that kind of a long-term bet.

I’ve been trying to YouTube-pill people in media for many years, as you know. You’ve been trying to undo the YouTube-pilling on your end, but I just think it’s clearly the most important media platform in the world right now. It’s a place where journalism has not historically had a central place.

If you were to look at YouTube as a whole and try to assess what piece of it is dedicated to what you or I would consider high-quality journalism, it’s a vanishingly small part of the overall ecosystem there.

So, part of my mission is just to crack that and figure out how to do YouTube and video in general in a way that is sustainable from an economic and a sort of creative standpoint. And then just to experiment and do a bunch of things.

This is not a face that needs to be on YouTube. So I’m also hoping to bring some other people in and nail some formats. But I look at what The Verge has done there. I look at what people like Joanna Stern and MKBHD have done there. To me, that is very exciting and it’s a space where there’s a lot less competition than text or podcasts.
Machine Gods is a podcast that you’re doing in partnership with NPR, which I want to talk about. But do you think of it as a YouTube product?

We want it to be video-first. What that means basically is that we are going to give a shit about what it looks like to a degree that we have not always done. We’re going to try to give people a lot of reasons to want to watch as well as listen.

Obviously, we know that there are some people who just don’t like video podcasts and so we want to give the audio audience something that is enjoyable, but this is the direction of things. You can’t do a podcast now without doing video on top of it. So we’re going to try to really embrace that and make a good version of it that is as good as two middle-aged journalists can pull off on YouTube.
Truly the future of media is middle-aged journalists pivoting to YouTube. I feel the same way because I’m now making more video and that’s what we’re doing. It’s going to be great.

The other reason to leave and to do this — and obviously people know I’m friends with Casey as well, and I’ve been talking to you and him about it for a long time — is that the AI story is here. There is a platform shift. There are new companies, new characters, new ideas to talk about in the world. It’s funny because in that context, usually you get a media shift as well. The way we tell stories or the formats we tell stories usually shifts alongside the thing we are talking about or the technology we’re talking about.

Here, YouTube feels like the most solid media foundation that exists. It’s the one that’s the same the most, even though it’s changing and it has YouTube Shorts and now you can A/B test everything, including your own face. But it’s the one that is the most the same. Instagram has undergone some massive change and it feels like that will continue happening.
Does it feel like YouTube is the most stable place to build as you’re trying to tell these new stories?

It does. I mean, obviously you never want to put all your eggs in one basket. So, we are also distributing video on Apple Podcasts and Spotify and we’re going to be everywhere. But yeah, it feels relatively stable.

The question I’m always wondering is what would it take to replace YouTube? Many companies have tried to replace YouTube, but to do that, you would not only have to build an experience that was better for creators and better for users, but you would also have to replicate the entire visual corpus of humanity. You would have to just get six million videos from plumbers about how to fix every individual sink and then upload it to that. It’s a really hard thing to displace. It is so ingrained for so many people, and I just think it’s going to keep growing.

We’ll come to this when we talk about AI, but a long time ago I asked Google CEO Sundar Pichai, “Well, what are you going to do if there’s no more websites?” And he was kind of like, “Well, we have YouTube.” And there’s just no arguing with that. You sure do. And it is just going to keep growing.
What has been the most surprising thing about going from The New York Times to what you might call the creator economy?

Well, we’re very new at it, but surprising to me so far is how much I like all the business stuff. I think in journalism, you’re always taught to stay in your lane, and I have never run a business before. Casey has run a business. I knew he enjoyed it. But for me, these are new muscles and I don’t enjoy all of it. Negotiating the insurance quotes for our defamation coverage is not what I would feel compelled by. But regarding actually running a business, there is something to this founder thing.

Yeah, it’s a good time. It’s funny, in talking to you and to Casey and Joanna, who also just left and started her own thing, that comes up a lot. From my perspective, it’s why I’ve been doing this a long time. What if I stopped running the business? That doesn’t seem to be a choice. This is the future of media — taking control of your business and taking control of your audience. There’s something very powerful there.

One of the things I want to talk about, and then I definitely want to talk about the book at length, is the audience for AI coverage, because I see it in two ways. There’s a group of people building the stuff that loves it and wants to consume all of it. There’s a group of people that truly hates it and thinks all of it is fake.

And then there’s what I would call an expanding group in the middle where the products have become more useful. You have to look at them and evaluate them as they are. They were not terribly useful a couple years ago. The promises did not match reality, but every day now it can do one more thing that it couldn’t do before. Whether that thing is hacking all of the websites in the world, we’ll set that aside, but AI can do things it couldn’t do before and the audience seems to be changing.
How are you thinking about the audience for Machine Gods and how it might grow or change?

I mean, right now we’re just trying a bunch of stuff that we think will be good and we hope that it will find its sort of natural audience. But I think you’re right that the audience is changing. I think for a while there was a lot of demand for cope — basically people telling you this is not happening, you don’t have to pay attention to it, it sucks, it’s hurting the environment.

There still is in some parts of the internet. YouTube has a weird amount of this still going on and Reddit is also very anti-AI. But I think most people, or at least maybe a plurality of people, are either resigned to or excited about the fact that this is not going away. That is the audience that we’re looking for.

We’re not trying to tell you that AI is amazing and we’re going to be in AI utopia under the new machine regime. We’re also not telling you that this stuff is fake and sucks and is going to go away on its own and so we don’t need to do anything to regulate it or be worried about it. Casey’s phrase for this is AI realism. He thinks there’s a big chunk of people who are just sort of curious and interested and maybe a little scared, but their reaction to the fear is not to try to bury their heads in the sand, but to try to understand the thing.

So we started feeling this when we were doing Hard Fork where we would do something that just seemed kind of not our vibe. We would do a Claude Code walkthrough tutorial where we would just spend half an hour building a website and film ourselves and throw it up and it would do great. So people clearly were curious, and even if the comments on the videos were all from people who hated AI, there was clearly a lot of demand out there for people who were just like, “I kind of want to know what’s going on.”
“I hate that I can’t stop watching this” is a real theme inside of AI coverage for a variety of reasons.

Let’s talk about the book. I think that’s going to frame a bunch of the other questions I have. The book is meticulously reported. It is really fun to read. And the point of it, as I’ve heard you describe it, is to tell the history of the deep learning revolution because all these people just talk in Signal and in extremely childish tweets.

Tell me about that gap because this is an industry that is obsessed with documenting itself for computers and being legible to computers and not at all to other people, which seems wild to me. So explain the reporting of this book, because it feels like convincing them to even tell you what happened was a slog.

It was, yeah. So basically the reason I wrote this is because I was scared that all of this stuff was going to disappear. I am a history buff. I love to read books about the Wright brothers or the electrification of rural America or the moments of great invention during the PC revolution. I’m such a sucker for that stuff.

What you notice as you read more of these books is just that they all rely on a lot of contemporaneous notes and evidence — the lab notes from the scientists developing the atomic bomb, the correspondence between the Wright brothers and their friends and business partners — that is preserved and archived.

It was just clear to me reporting on AI every day that there was not going to be anything remotely similar for this stuff because A, all the people building this stuff work for private companies. They’re not government employees who are legally required to preserve their correspondence. And B, the Signal messages and Slack messages are all set by the lawyers to auto-delete after a certain period. So there was literally going to be kind of a mass disappearance with each passing year of these, I think, historically important artifacts, moments, and stories.

And then C, the researchers are all too busy to keep notes. They’re all grinding because they’re trying to build the machine god. So, I thought as a journalist, but more so almost as a historian, which is not a role I’ve ever officially played, but one I think I was playing with this book. I was just like, “I’ve got to just get this stuff because I have this sort of privileged ringside seat. These people talk to me. I know some of them will sit down and talk to me and tell me the stories.”

We did a lot of it on background so they could be protected from the consequences of talking to me. But this was sort of my attempt to furiously get all the stuff and put it in the archive where future generations could look at it.

The theme that really jumps out at me as I read the book was there’s a moment when AGI goes from being a thing they’re all dreaming about to being a thing that they all have to build and the shackles come off and they say, “We have to do this,” and they all drive toward it as hard as they can.

You talk specifically about Google where the Overton window moved and suddenly the people inside of Google, who thought this was all a pipe dream and pretty silly, started talking about AGI. That moment feels like the single most important moment in the history of AI, where “Won’t it be great?” goes to “We better go as fast as we can.”
Talk about that a little bit, because that shift inside these companies feels under-reported.

Yeah, I think that’s absolutely right. I mean, people have been talking and writing about AGI or some precursor that wasn’t called AGI but meant the same thing since literally antiquity. And especially since the 1950s, when the term artificial intelligence was born, people were talking about it. Alan Turing was writing about the thinking machine that could do anything the human brain could.

So this concept has been around for a long time, but there was no technology anywhere on the market or in research labs that could actually do what people wanted it to do — that could take in information, learn to learn about that information, and then use that to make predictions and act in the world. People tried lots of different ways to do this and none of them worked all that well.

What really needed to happen was the transformer needed to come along. This architecture that Google developed in 2017 and published and then presented to, among other places, OpenAI, which took the idea of the transformer and ran with it. And that’s the T in ChatGPT today. But that was the–
Somewhere a Google PR person just leapt out of a bush to hand you a check.
They do love this line.
They love it when you say it. They get so happy.
They love it. They love it less when you point out that although they invented it, they absolutely failed to turn it into a product until after OpenAI did.

But yeah, it was a dream, but there was nothing to attach to the dream. There was no technology. And then the large language model came and suddenly it was like, “Oh, maybe this is the thing that could scale forever and keep improving over many orders of magnitude.” So, that’s the light bulb that goes off at OpenAI and then later at Google is like, “Now we have the tool to do the thing that we have always wanted to do.”

You’ve got a line in there where you just point out that next-token prediction has not failed yet — that it is doing all the things people want it to do. We’ve obviously had to develop lots of technology around it. There are harnesses to make agents work. There’s reinforcement learning. There’s all this stuff around it. But that core technology has scaled.

The reason I bring that up is that in 2023 into 2024, I would ask every AI person who would come on the show or that we would see on The Verge whether LLMs can do it. Can they do the thing you want them to do? Because I don’t think at that moment it was clear that they could.

We’re closer now. They’re all openly talking about AGI. We are watching Meta’s Muse just walk its little butt around the internet whenever it wants. Do you think LLMs can do it? Do you think they can get there?

I think they can. I’m not certain about that, but they’ve been shockingly good and effective so far. If you go back and you look at the first LLMs, it’s just like 99 percent of people thought this is crazy, that this won’t scale. And then it just keeps working at every stage, at every order of magnitude. I’ve asked people, what was it about next-token prediction that was clearly superior to everything that came before it? There have been people who have told me this actually exists in the human brain too. There’s a whole school of thought that says that what is happening inside the human brain is essentially next-token prediction at scale. Obviously, it’s more complicated. These are not one-for-one replicas of each other.

But I think this is the fundamental mystery at the heart of AI: why is next-token prediction so remarkably effective? I think we don’t know. I kind of think it’s one of these cosmic mysteries, but why all of this works is because next-token prediction turns out to generalize really, really, really well.

There’s a part of that where all these companies had to believe it. Dario Amodei of Anthropic obviously wrote his paper, “Big Blob of Compute,” where he said you can just do it. You can just dump data and compute at this and we’ll get there. Everyone else had to be convinced of this.
What path did the AI companies all take to be convinced of this, and are they all fully convinced of it now?

I don’t think they’re all fully convinced of it now. I think they are convinced of it to varying degrees. Ilya Sutskever has this phrase, “Feel the AGI,” that he would walk floor to floor at OpenAI chanting in the old days and reminding people to feel the AGI. I think the labs feel the AGI to varying degrees. I think Anthropic is clearly the most AGI-pilled of the labs, with OpenAI kind of a close second.

And then there’s Google, which I think has always struggled to feel the AGI. I think there are lots of reasons for that, but it’s very funny. I love this section of the book where there’s this internal memo battle at Google, where they would just go on their internal message boards and Googlers love to write these manifestos and then snipe at each other’s manifestos and things like that.
a688eb73dc8e2807: AI has yet to deliver any financial payoff to US businesses outside of the tech sector, according to investment biz Apollo Global Management.

The global asset firm made the claim in a posting to its Daily Spark blog that features analysis on the US economy and capital markets. It says corporate America is starting to view token spending not as a source of growth, but rather as a cost center that weighs on company margins.

Apollo’s chief economist Torsten Slok says that revenue per worker may be rising for the so-called "Magnificent Seven" tech firms, which includes the hyperscalers plus Apple, Nvidia and Tesla, but this isn't the case for the rest of the S&P 500 businesses.
The same goes for profit margins, and for AI boosting corporate productivity growth, he adds, posting charts to back up these claims.

Apollo's assertion has met with pushback from some, who commented on social media that they did not recognize the picture painted by Slok. Others said a similar effect was noted in the PC industry, when productivity growth lagged the widespread adoption of computers in business by a decade or more.

However the investment firm’s observations chime with various reports The Register has analyzed over the past year or two, such as one earlier this year from PwC that found the majority of chief executives had enjoyed neither increased revenue nor decreased costs from AI, despite investing heavily in the technology.

Research from professional services firm Deloitte also showed that adopting AI tools has not helped the bottom line for most companies, while a separate report found AI is now facing corporate accountability after several years of investment with little or no return, and projects will have to prove their worth or be axed.

McKinsey reckons the corporate world is now at a turning point and on the road to seeing a return for all the effort that organizations have put into pilots and early AI deployments – although it concedes the number of businesses reporting an actual earnings boost from their AI initiatives has remained flat.
Slok questions whether mainstream corporations will ever be able to turn AI projects into higher revenue growth and higher profit margins, despite the appearance of cheaper or open-sourced models.

In business, intelligence is mostly judgment, he says, and therefore depends on context. He notes that AI does not really understand anything, but especially accountability, trust, culture, unwritten rules, ethical trade-offs or fairness, all of which shape companies' reputational risk and ultimately drive revenue growth and profit margins.

Apollo also notes a slowdown in token spending growth, claiming this shows the spending is highly price-sensitive and demand falls away or switches to cheap open source alternatives in response to even modest increases in cost. This casts doubt over the economics of pouring billions into constructing ever more datacenters if the resulting compute is only likely to turn a marginal profit.

The investment biz previously handed $11 billion to Intel in exchange for a 49 percent stake in the chipmaker’s Fab 34 manufacturing plant at Leixlip in Ireland. Intel repurchased Apollo’s stake earlier this year for $14.2 billion after the chipmaker had put itself back on firmer financial ground. ®
045c951ec904c7db: NEW YORK: Hollywood icon Sylvester Stallone has revealed that his biggest financial windfalls have come from his art collection rather than his blockbuster film roles.
The Rocky star explained that he reinvested his acting paycheques into fine art back in the 1980s, buying pieces that later skyrocketed in value.
Today, several masterworks hanging in his home are worth over US$40 million (about RM168 million) each.
Speaking on The Overlap podcast, the veteran actor confessed that collecting art remains his main passion.
He highlighted his investments in legendary masters alongside modern talents.
"That's my weakness. Art. I do own a lot more contemporary artists who are becoming the new greats. George Condo, Rashid Johnson, they're this generation's Picassos," Stallone said.
When asked about the value of his prized Picasso and Warhol pieces, he noted: "About US$40 million for just one."
Reflecting on his entry into the art market during the mid-1980s, Stallone recalled buying works by Impressionist and modern masters at a fraction of today's prices.
This included Monets for US$130,000 (around RM546,000) and Francis Bacon paintings for US$75,000 (about RM315,000).
While he made substantial profits by selling pieces for millions at the time, he regretted parting with them too soon.
"Ten years later, 12 years later, guys come back and try to sell it to me for US$75 million (around RM315 million). I'm not joking," he said.

He offered a piece of advice for fellow collectors: "So the point is, if you've got art, don't sell it unless you've got to pay the mortgage because it's appreciating. It doesn't cost you anything; you don't have to feed it."
Stallone cited one notable example involving a piece from Claude Monet's Haystacks series.
He originally bought the painting for around US$110,000 (around RM462,000), only for a dealer to offer it back to him years later for an eye-watering US$130 million (approximately RM546 million).

With his historical art holdings virtually irreplaceable at current market values, Stallone has now turned his focus to collecting rare vintage timepieces, particularly rare hand-painted Rolex models.
d4ea8e48279e944e: KUALA LUMPUR: Swimmer Jayden Tan wants to compete at the World Short Course Championships in Beijing, but his dentistry studies could stand in the way.
Jayden faces the prospect of missing almost two weeks of classes to represent Malaysia at the world meet, leaving him weighing how to juggle both commitments.
He clocked four minutes 16.48 seconds in the men's 400m individual medley at the recent National Short Course Championships, finishing 1.10s inside the Beijing B qualifying standard of 4:17.58.
The effort was also just 0.39 seconds outside his own national record of 4:16.09.
"Right now, it's tough to juggle both, but I do think it's possible. I'll just have to see how I manage my time," said Jayden.
"Dentistry is quite a tough course, but it's not impossible. I'll take it one thing at a time."
With classes running from 9am to 5pm, finding time to train is already a challenge.
"If I go to Beijing, I'll skip almost two weeks of school, which is quite a lot. So I'll just have to see."
Jayden said he had already met the qualifying standard before the national meet.
His latest effort came despite taking almost two weeks off swimming after the Asian Games and resuming training only just before the competition.
"I think the break was actually quite helpful. I only started training this Monday and I was quite surprised with the results."
The narrow record miss has given Jayden another incentive to make the Beijing trip, where he believes he can go faster.
"I really do want to go because it's such a big meet, it's the World Championships. It would be a good feeling to break it. I'll do my best and see what I can do to make it to Beijing."
482676e92c742897: MANCHESTER: Winless in eight games and hovering just above the Premier League relegation zone, struggling Manchester United are facing the prospect of yet another managerial change, with Michael Carrick likely to pay the price.
The former United midfielder was warmly applauded by fans as he made his way down the tunnel after his team's chastening 3-0 defeat by Bournemouth at Old Trafford on Sunday.
Moments later, a chorus of boos erupted as the players left the pitch - with fans clear in their minds where the blame lies for United's current malaise.

Carrick was handed a two-year deal in May after inspiring an impressive revival following the team's struggles under Ruben Amorim - United secured third place in the Premier League and a return to the Champions League.
However, a drastic decline this season is an all-too-familiar story for United supporters, who last witnessed a Premier League title triumph 13 years ago under Alex Ferguson.
An emotional Carrick denied his lap of the pitch at full-time on Sunday was a goodbye as he struggles to come to terms with his team's precipitous decline.
"I definitely knew that we hadn't cracked it and there was a lot of work to be done, but that doesn't mean to say that it should have gone this way," he said.
Carrick, 45, is clinging on but his position appears increasingly precarious, with former Newcastle boss Eddie Howe and ex-Germany boss Julian Nagelsmann apparently in the frame for the job.
The United boss, who won multiple titles in the club's golden era under Ferguson, was the seventh permanent appointment since the Scot retired.
David Moyes was proven in the Premier League, Louis van Gaal and Jose Mourinho had stellar records and Erik ten Hag and Amorim were seen as rising stars of coaching.
Sentimental choice

Carrick is in the same category as Ole Gunnar Solskjaer, who was in charge for three years from 2018 - a sentimental choice as a former player who played a major role in the club's glory years under Ferguson.

"The Manchester United fans are singing the Michael Carrick song because I think they know what's going to happen here. They've seen this before. He's one of their own and he's popular," former United captain Gary Neville told Sky Sports.
"But the owners, the sporting department and the players are not popular and they've badly let this football club down," Neville said.
The problems at the club, as Neville points out, go far beyond the dugout.
Despite fierce, ongoing protests from fans, the US-based Glazer family still hold a majority stake in the club Malcolm Glazer bought via a leveraged takeover in 2005, saddling United with huge debts.
Any hopes that the arrival of British billionaire Jim Ratcliffe as a minority owner in 2024 would signal a new dawn have been dashed.
Ratcliffe has overseen cost-cutting measures including widespread redundancies and ticket hikes but the club's debt has still soared above £1.1 billion (US$1.47 billion).

United, who for years bullied their rivals in the transfer market, lost out on the biggest names as they targeted a summer midfield rebuild, with Elliot Anderson, Sandro Tonali and Mateus Fernandes all choosing other clubs.
United instead recruited Carlos Baleba, Youri Tielemans and Andrey Santos -- none of whom have made a strong impression - for combined fees of about £150 million.
Significant rifts have emerged in recent weeks.
Lisandro Martinez criticised director of football Jason Wilcox for not doing more to strengthen Carrick's squad.
Last week captain Bruno Fernandes publicly questioned Carrick's tactics in a 4-1 humbling by Champions League debutants Como.
Carrick is expected to take the blame, but the route back to the top for one of the world's biggest clubs appears tougher than ever.
"It can't just be the manager again. There has got to be consequences above that. You can't keep letting the people pick the manager who keep getting it wrong," Neville said.
"It's years now without a Premier League title. That will be another five or 10 before you know it because there are other clubs set up for success and Manchester United aren't," Neville added.

ea5a2a46042a7fb9: KUALA LUMPUR: The disqualification of long jumper Nazmi Nasri — who subsequently missed out on a silver medal — at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Para Games for failing to comply with shoe specifications, should serve as a major lesson for the Malaysian contingent.

"In my view, this was unintentional. The matter will be brought to the National Sports Council, Paralympic Council of Malaysia and National Sports Institute for analysis and discussion on preventive measures.
"We hope this will not happen again at future sporting events," he said at a press conference recently.
