126cf3a97980bffe: RIYADH: Yemen's Houthis have kept up their attacks on Saudi Arabia as senior officials from the kingdom, Turkey and Pakistan are due to hold high-stakes talks with Iran in Tehran on Monday, following warnings of a return to war.
Fresh explosions rattled Riyadh overnight, along with a text message warning to residents, after the Iran-allied Houthis claimed a new attack on the Saudi capital's international airport on Sunday.
Saudi Arabia, the world's top oil exporter, has become deeply embroiled in the eight-month war since hostilities in its long-running conflict with the Iran-allied Houthis resumed in July.
Defence minister Prince Khalid bin Salman is among the delegations travelling to Tehran, made up of officials from the three countries that signed a defence alliance in Mecca in August.
Their visit follows warnings by the US, Iran and Israel that hostilities could resume.

Tensions have increased ahead of Israel's pivotal election on Tuesday and next week's US mid-terms, where US president Donald Trump's Republicans are battling to keep control of both chambers of the US Congress.

Iran's security chief Mohsen Rezaei will take part in Monday's meeting with Prince Khalid, Pakistani army chief General Asim Munir and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin, the deputy secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, Ali Bagheri Kani, told state TV.

"This historic meeting in Tehran may be the last chance before escalation spirals out of control, an attempt to impose a path of de-escalation before it's too late," Hesham Alghannam, a Saudi security analyst and researcher, posted on X.
"The presence of military and security figures at this level together means that the remaining time is extremely limited," Alghannam said.
'Serious tensions'

On Sunday, as blasts rang out over Riyadh and authorities sent texts warning residents of a "hostile aerial threat", the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis said it struck missile launchers and storage facilities in Yemen.
The Houthis said they had attacked Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport once again.
The repeatedly targeted facility has been largely closed since 13 people were killed and more than 300 wounded in a major attack this month.
Mediation efforts between the US and Iran have been led by Qatar and Pakistan.
A Qatari delegation visited Tehran on Sunday, Iran's foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei said.
"Our region is in the grip of serious tensions, and neighbouring countries are striving to convey a message and put forward initiatives," Baqaei said on Monday.
Andreas Krieg of London-based risk consultancy MENA analytica said Prince Khalid's presence in Tehran was "hugely significant", calling him the "strategic mastermind of Saudi Arabia".
Prince Khalid, brother of Saudi de facto ruler Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, has emerged as one of Saudi Arabia's key diplomatic interlocutors, dispatched on sensitive regional missions.
"For him to go to Iran directly in this very sensitive time is a very, very strong signal that the kingdom is not just... sitting and waiting for things, events to unfold," Krieg told AFP.
"There's a clear effort by the Mecca alliance to signal to Iran that they're ready to work together to defend the kingdom and defend the kingdom's borders," he added.
"And so should Iran think to escalate, which they will likely do if Israel and the US strikes, and they will most likely strike Saudi Arabia, Iran will have to bear the consequences."
'Don't test us'
Comments by senior officials have raised speculation about renewed hostilities.
Iran's foreign minister Abbas Araghchi said on Sunday "there has been talk of a new war" but that Tehran's policies remain unchanged.
Trump said on Friday that Washington "may do another little Epic Fury", referring to the US-Israeli campaign against Iran that began on Feb 28.
On Sunday, Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu warned that Iran may try to disrupt the Israeli elections, where he is in a close-fought race to stay in power.
"We have intelligence signs that our enemies, Iran and its proxies, could challenge us with attacks in order to disrupt the elections," Netanyahu said.
"Don't test us. You will suffer disproportionate blows," added Netanyahu, who has campaigned heavily on his security credentials.

The remarks came as Israel's Channel 12, citing unnamed sources, reported a confrontation between Netanyahu and army chief Eyal Zamir over an unspecified new directive in the war with Iran, which the premier denied.
b742880571a92210: We've spent the past several decades using duct tape, string, and chewing gum to chain the world's computers together into this thing we call the internet, so there's really no good reason to be surprised that most of it is full of software containing vulnerabilities that are practically just as old.

You can listen to the latest episode of The Kettle right here on this page, as well as on Spotify, Apple Music, or YouTube. Those platforms also let you subscribe to Kettle, so you are always notified when the latest episode goes live.

The world is still reeling from the PHP2Shell revelations that hit the news cycle this week, and on The Kettle there's no better topic for host Brandon Vigliarolo, cybersecurity editor Jessica Lyons, and FOSS reporter Liam Proven to tease apart.

Join us to discuss what exactly is going on, how AI was key to finding another issue no human likely ever would have discovered on their own, and why exposing more bad code in the backbone of the world's computers might be just what we need to rethink the whole thing for the better.

Hi everyone, and welcome to the latest episode of The Register's Kettle podcast. I'm your host, Reg reporter Brandon Vigliarolo. And hey, there's only one thing we could focus on for this week's episode, given all the hubbub around it, and that's the PHP apocalypse. It turns out most of the internet is running software that could allow remote code execution on host systems via a pair, or as of today apparently three, vulnerabilities that have come to collectively be known as PHP2Shell. So that's not great. With me to talk about this is our security editor Jessica Lyons and open source reporter Liam Proven, who has a few things to say about PHP itself and why it's probably not surprising we're finding ourselves in this mess. Thanks to you both for coming on.
So Jess, let's start with the basics. What is this? How big of a problem is it? And where do we stand on getting things fixed?

Great. The short answer is it's a very big problem. So we have these two related memory safety vulnerabilities, and they are in the PHP core. Collectively they're called PHP2Shell, and they affect every version that's been released in the last decade affected by one or both of these, going back to about version 5.4. So the general consensus is this is about 70 percent of all of the websites on the internet are running this code. So it basically affects everyone at this point.

What happened here is that this dates actually back to August. An independent researcher first spotted this, and then we can talk a little bit more later about who found more of the exploits and what the (PHP) Foundation did with that. But so he found this vulnerability. There was a coordinated disclosure process with the PHP Foundation, and then that broke a little bit starting over the weekend, and then onto Monday, there were some leaks. There was a video posted that purported to show this exploit. And so we get this emergency warning from the PHP Foundation late Monday saying, "Hey, we are going to be releasing these emergency patches, so everybody get ready so you can implement them as soon as possible. It's very serious." So by Wednesday, they did release these, and there's this mass attempt to patch before any of the attackers get a hold of this and are able to attack websites with it. And one of the issues too is that some websites are running really, really old versions and so they aren't able to patch. So they're just sitting there, these legacy servers are still vulnerable.
So there's no direct update path for those old versions, right? It's basically shut this down and reinstall it kind of thing.

Exactly. So basically they're both these memory corruption vulnerabilities and by exploiting them, an attacker can kind of shape the memory that PHP trusts. And then they can use that to hijack what happens next. And that can mean remote code execution. They can take over the websites, they can steal data. And so people are visiting these websites they trust and they don't realize that the underlying code is stealing their data or delivering malware to their computer. And again, this is potentially 70 percent of the internet. So it's a big deal.

Quite a few sites were offline. I know even some big services. I stopped playing because I had a baby, but I used to play Final Fantasy XIV pretty religiously. And I know that the entire login server was offline a couple days ago

They were like, "You've got to fix this. Sorry, no one can play the game. If you're not logged in right now, you're not getting logged in for the foreseeable future." It's just insane how much of the internet was affected by this. Now It's under exploit, is that correct? But maybe not successfully exploited yet?

Right. So after the patches were released on Wednesday, later Wednesday, AWS came out and said, "We've seen exploitation attempts at least four days before the patches were released." So that kind of caused another frenzy that, "My God, it's under attack, the whole internet is on fire." There haven't been any successful attacks to date. There's been a ton of attempts.

There's a lot of POCs; some work, some don't. But as of Friday, according to the Foundation and according to all of the security experts that I've spoken to, we haven't seen any evidence of successful exploitation. I don't think that means we're in the clear. I think it just means it's taking a while for people – and honestly AIs – to develop successful attacks, but that's where we are right now.
Because it's a complicated attack chain, correct?

So basically, right. This is not working yet, but especially with some of these older websites that are running older versions of PHP that are going to have to take a more thorough approach to getting this fixed and possibly going down for some time, this could be one of those problems that remains serious for a while. And let's not forget, 70 percent of the websites on the internet, that's almost three-quarters of the entire internet. I don't know how many hundreds of thousands or millions of sites that is, but some of those are probably never going to get patched.
Just the way it goes. Right. This is going to be the sort of thing that we end up hearing about months or years from now.
I'm sure there'll be some bank somewhere that eventually ends up getting – we'll hear about some breach disclosure letter from the state of Maine in four or five years.
And local governments, federal and state governments, I think these are the ones that we're going to be hearing about quite a while from now.

Because that's one of the things I was thinking about even for me in my tiny little town in northern Michigan. I wonder if my township or the county is going to be all over it to update their PHP server. Does their IT guy, who probably is a retired dude who lives in the area, even know this is a problem? It really is one of those things that is a big deal, but if you're not kind of following the news on this, it could probably go completely unnoticed. And for many websites, I'm sure it will.

So, it's pretty crazy. Liam, you're working on a story, I think, as we are recording this, about some of the history of PHP and how it really probably wasn't very well designed or intended to become so ubiquitous on the internet. What's going on there?

I've seen one angle on this, which is people saying, "This is 1990s code and it has 1990s problems," which is one way to look at it. But I'm a 1980s internet guy; that's when I started exploring it. My primary email address is older than the web, and it still works.

My gods, it gets a lot of spam, but it still works. I've watched the rise and rise of PHP since the first releases. Now, I have no personal interest in web development. I can program, but I don't because I'm really bad at it and nobody needs to have my code inflicted upon them. The guy that wrote PHP in the first place, Rasmus Lerdorf, is my age. I've never met him; I'm sure he's a nice guy. But he said in a very early interview about it, "I really don't like programming. I built this tool to program less so that I could just reuse code." And that was about 1993. He built a little tool that allowed him to put macros in HTML for his own website, and it's just grown. In a later interview, he said something along the lines of, "I don't know anything about writing programming languages. I'm just improvising this as I go and people seem to like it."

It originally stood for "Personal Home Page," I think, and later was given a recursive acronym of "PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor." This is a programming language that you mix in with the HTML of a website. It predates the modern model of building websites where a database contains the text and a content management system of some kind assembles on the fly the pages that each person sees. This is an older model where you're running programs that are part of the markup language, which was not a good idea, but that was how he did it.

There was a lovely blog post. I've got an old friend who's an extremely skilled and talented programmer who has built a career on PHP, and he said to me, "Look, those criticisms that you've mentioned are of the really early versions and it's changed now." And if he hears this, he's going to be cross with me. But my favorite summary was from a blog called Eev.ee way back when that called PHP "a fractal of bad design."

Whatever level you look at it, it was done badly. If you look at the whole plan of "let's just intermingle program code in with the markup language," not a good idea. If you look at the details of how it was implemented, not a good idea. If you look down at low-level details of how the functions return values, not a good idea: inconsistent syntax, inconsistent functions, functions that do really weird things, by default no stack traces, not great error reporting.

Now, I'm sure a lot of this has been papered over now, but really there is one reason PHP is still around and still so big: Zuck. Facebook was built in PHP. And Facebook makes lots and lots of money and it's been throwing money at making PHP faster and more reliable and more scalable for decades.
Brandon (11:03) Have they been big contributors to it?

Liam (11:06) Yeah. They even built a compiler for it, which I suspect is still in use. Now, how much of Facebook today is in PHP? I don't know, possibly none, but for a long time basically the world's biggest and busiest public-facing website that wasn't owned by Google – only because Google have failed to ever make a successful social network – was built on PHP. And it's big, it's complicated. Like Linux itself, nobody fully understands how the whole thing works anymore and hasn't probably for decades.

And now people have got bots that they can throw against it and ask them to analyze it. I think this is probably just the first, and I think there's going to be many more. A friend of mine who's a senior developer had a look at the patch, and he's not a C guy, but he said – I'm quoting from comments on Mastodon – that the patch to the current version is 13,000 lines of C. That's a doozy of a patch.

A bunch of people have been working like crazy for quite some time. Some people who've looked at this say it looks handwritten to me. Others have said, "No, I think this is bot-generated." I think the truth is probably a bit of both: some from one, some from the other.
Bit of both. I mean, you can't pump out thirteen thousand lines that quickly and have it tested. God, I hope they tested it.

Right. But that's just for the current version, and this hole affects every published version. So if they do manage to fix this one, how long till the next one comes along? Because I think there's going to be –

Especially with the speed at which vulnerabilities are being discovered now. I feel like every time I turn around, I've written one Patch Tuesday article in the past few months, and that one broke the previous two records. And I think since then every month has included more patches, and a lot of those are probably –
October at this point is the record: over a thousand for Microsoft alone. So, yep.
That's insane. Like you said, it is a fractal of bad design all the way down, and is going to probably have more vulnerabilities discovered.
Seventy percent of all websites on the internet are using this. What can we do? Are we stuck?

Panel tiga hakim yang dipengerusikan oleh Hakim Alwi Abdul Wahab, bersama-sama Shahnaz Sulaiman dan Ong Chee Kwan, sebulat suara membenarkan rayuan SL Land Sdn Bhd dan Foong Wei Ching terhadap JMB yang menguruskan Sentral Bazar di Nilai, Negeri Sembilan.

Mahkamah mengetepikan keputusan Mahkamah Tinggi terdahulu yang mengekalkan kuasa JMB mengenakan syarat kemasukan terhadap pemilik ingkar di bawah Peraturan-Peraturan Pengurusan Strata (Penyenggaraan dan Pengurusan) 2015.

Ketika membacakan alasan penghakiman ringkas, Ong berkata, peraturan itu memperincikan tindakan yang boleh diambil oleh JMB terhadap pemilik ingkar, termasuk menyahaktifkan kad akses, mewajibkan mereka menandatangani buku daftar apabila meminta bantuan untuk keluar masuk bangunan, serta menggantung penggunaan kemudahan dan perkhidmatan bersama.
Bagaimanapun, tindakan sedemikian tidak memberi kuasa kepada JMB untuk melarang seseorang pemilik daripada memasuki unitnya sendiri.

Tambahnya, peruntukan undang-undang yang jelas diperlukan bagi memberi kuasa sedemikian, namun tiada sebarang peruntukan seumpamanya wujud.
Panel hakim mengisytiharkan tindakan enggan membenarkan pengarah dan ejen sah SL Land memasuki unit mereka pada 4 Mei dan 20 Jun 2023 sebagai menyalahi undang-undang.
Mahkamah turut memutuskan bahawa syarat yang mewajibkan kehadiran atau kebenaran pemegang saham syarikat sebelum dibenarkan masuk juga tidak dibenarkan oleh undang-undang.

Sehubungan itu, mahkamah mengeluarkan perintah injunksi bagi menghalang JMB daripada menyekat laluan masuk, sambil mengekalkan kuasanya di bawah peraturan berkaitan serta peraturan keselamatan munasabah dan tanpa diskriminasi yang terpakai bagi semua pemilik petak.
Mahkamah turut mengetepikan perintah kos RM30,000 oleh Mahkamah Tinggi dan menganugerahkan ganti rugi nominal kepada SL Land memandangkan syarikat itu tidak membuktikan sebarang kerugian ketara.
JMB diperintahkan membayar kos keseluruhan berjumlah RM50,000 bagi prosiding di kedua-dua mahkamah.
Peguam Ivanpal Singh Grewal, Harwinder Kaur dan S Nisha mewakili SL Land dan Foong, manakala K Muralidharan dan Ahmad Amir Mukhlis bertindak bagi pihak JMB.

2c570a25fafb0da3: PUTRAJAYA, Oct 26 — Malaysia’s third offer to assist Nepal in its search and rescue (SAR) operations for mud flood victims was accepted after two earlier offers were turned down, paving the way for the deployment of the Special Malaysia Disaster Assistance and Rescue Team (SMART), equipped with technical expertise and advanced detection equipment.

SMART commander Senior Fire Superintendent 1 Abdul Manaf Che Isa, who led the mission, said Malaysia initially offered to send 50 rescuers, followed by a second offer of 25 personnel with SAR equipment, but Nepal declined both offers because it already had sufficient rescue teams.

He said Nepal’s government eventually accepted Malaysia’s third offer, which involved deploying just 11 SMART personnel, nine high-capacity drones and specialised detection equipment, after several rounds of discussions.

“Our initial offer was to deploy 50 personnel for SAR operations, but Nepal had already deployed its own rescue teams and declined the offer. The Nepalese government needed specialised equipment and expertise that it lacked.
“At the same time, we did not want to travel there only to find that there was no work for us to do,” he said in a recent interview with Bernama on SMART’s humanitarian mission in Nepal.

According to Abdul Manaf, Nepal declined the first two offers not because it did not need Malaysia’s assistance, but because it had already mobilised enough rescuers, including members of the military, police and fire services, volunteers, and international SAR teams from countries including China and South Korea.

He said SMART’s strengths included high-capacity drones for aerial surveys, mapping disaster-hit areas and locating victims, as well as specialised equipment capable of detecting sounds and movement beneath mud deposits.

“Buildings may be buried beneath mud while their structures remain intact. The area may look clear from above, but this equipment enables us to detect sounds and movement. Such equipment was not available there, and the authorities saw the need for it,” he said.

Abdul Manaf said diplomatic engagement through the Malaysian Embassy in Kathmandu also played a key role in convincing the Nepalese military that SMART could provide the technical assistance needed, including SAR detection equipment, search cameras, satellite phones and specialised communication systems.

He said the Nepalese government prioritised self-sufficient international relief teams, a criterion that aligned with SMART’s capabilities recognised by the International Search and Rescue Advisory Group (INSARAG), as disaster victims need local shelter, food supplies and logistical support.

Once Nepal’s government had approved the mission, the SMART team was deployed to the Nepalese military’s tactical base in Trishuli, from where it took a helicopter to reach search areas no longer accessible by road because of infrastructure damage.

Abdul Manaf said the mud floods had drastically altered the terrain, making existing maps unreliable and forcing SMART personnel to use drones, GPS, and physical observations to determine search routes.

“For ground operations, we could not rely fully on maps as the terrain had changed significantly from what they depicted. Roads and buildings had been destroyed, leaving only rocks, sand and mud,” he said, noting that mud deposits reached depths of three to five metres, and up to eight metres in some areas.

He said heavy rain and overcast conditions also hampered helicopter operations, forcing personnel to be dropped off on hillsides before walking for more than an hour to reach the operation site, while also facing the risk of further disasters.

He said SMART personnel spent three days conducting secondary searches with Nepalese military tactical teams in designated sectors between Timure and Syabrubesi, using their expertise and specialised equipment to search the last known location of the Malaysians reported missing, but found no survivors.
SMART also shared aerial images and drone footage with the families concerned and handed over equipment and supplies to the Nepalese military to support continued search operations.

Abdul Manaf stressed that the SMART team had searched as extensively as possible amid difficult geographical, weather and safety conditions, adding that SAR operations focused first on rescuing survivors, with recovery efforts undertaken if necessary.
He also appealed to the families to remain resilient and patient while awaiting further steps by the Malaysian and Nepalese governments through coordination by the Foreign Ministry. — Bernama
4d7ae43f5123f82f: FORT KENT, Oct 26 — In the heat of US midterm elections, President Donald Trump’s tariffs on Canada—and Ottawa’s retaliation—have taken centrestage in timber-producing Maine, walloped by the economic fallout perhaps more than any other state.

Residents in Maine’s frontier towns express worry that the tariffs have also triggered a rupture in cross-border relationships built up over decades, and that the intricate community fabric could take years to repair.
“Tariffs are definitely, economically, going to hurt us here” in northern Maine, brewery co-owner Shawn Pelletier said in Caribou, a city with extensive ties to Canada’s New Brunswick province.
Maine is reluctantly on the front lines of the trade war which saw Trump last year slap tariffs of up to 50 per cent on some Canadian goods, including logging equipment and some wood products.

Many logging operations in the nation’s most heavily-forested state are suffering, and cross-border tourism has tanked. Households already struggling with fuel prices are seeing costs of living soar, an issue dominating the midterms.

Ahead of the November 3 vote to decide who controls the US Congress, tensions are up in the port-of-entry town of Fort Kent and Maine’s other border stations where two million Americans and Canadians cross every year.
“We’re worried they hate us,” a Maine retiree sitting with friends told AFP in Fort Kent, as she nodded towards Canada, visible across the Saint John River.
‘Ripple’ effect
Figures show the economic pain has already arrived and is “far-reaching,” according to Garrett Martin, president of the nonpartisan Maine Center for Economic Policy (MECEP).

Because Maine shares “a long history with Canada, and intertwined both family and business relationships, I think there are a lot of ways in which we are potentially being hurt even more” by the tariff impact, Martin told AFP.
Canadian visits to Maine plunged 43 per cent in the tariffs’ first year, depressing shop sales and tax revenue, he said.
And in Maine’s US$8-billion forest-related industry, “we’re seeing cost increases ripple through,” with some logging operations shrinking or shuttering altogether, Martin said.

Logging has been in a slump for years, with eight pulp and paper mills closing in Maine since 2012, according to Dana Doran, executive director of the Professional Logging Contractors of the Northeast (PLC).
Now tariffs on trucks, logging equipment, parts and wood products are sending prices “up 30 to 50 per cent across the board,” Doran told AFP.
High diesel costs have only darkened the scenario.

A truck carrying softwood lumber is weighted at the ‘Pleasant River Lumber’ sawmill in Enfield, Maine, on October 13, 2026. In the heat of US midterm elections, President Donald Trump’s tariffs on Canada, and Ottawa’s retaliation, have taken centrestage in timber-producing Maine, walloped by the economic fallout perhaps more than any other state. — AFP pic
‘Friction’
For two centuries, Canadian mills near Maine have processed vast amounts of its timber.
The border communities are linked through business and families, but “the tariff conversation I think has added friction to that situation, which is unfortunate,” Doran said.
Canada, by far Maine’s top trading partner, retaliated against Washington in September with tariffs of 25-50 percent on US lumber, wood furniture and more.
Maine-based companies, particularly producers of hardwood, “rely heavily on those Canadian markets,” Doran said.
Not all Maine loggers are upset. Pleasant River Lumber Company is producing 110 million board feet of softwood lumber per year at its main sawmill in Enfield and aims to expand production.
In a forest grove to the east, a contractor climbed into a mechanical harvester and pivoted its head to grip and fell a tree, strip its branches and cut the trunk into exact lengths.
“The margins are so thin that you can’t make a lot of mistakes,” a logging manager said.
On a tour of the highly-automated sawmill, co-owner Jason Brochu told AFP that US tariffs and duties have created a level playing field to compete with Canada’s subsidized lumber operations.
“We’re a glaring example of how trade protection works and how it’s beneficial,” said Brochu.
Either way, the trade war is causing political headaches.
Trump on Friday announced a tariff pause for Canadian wood products and some other imports, a last-minute move critics interpreted as seeking to aid Republicans in tight midterm races.
In a scrappy battle for a US Senate seat, Maine incumbent Susan Collins sought to take credit for securing those exemptions.
Her Democratic challenger Troy Jackson, himself a former logger, argued Collins merely “enabled this chaos” brought by Trump’s tariffs.
How long such instability lasts is unknown.
“It’s going to take a long time to rebuild the trust” between Mainers and Canadians, said the MECEP’s Garrett. — AFP
33d80bce796280f3: DAKAR, Oct 26 — Signs across the Senegalese capital proclaim 'Africa welcomes, Dakar celebrates' ahead of the Youth Olympic Games, which will mark the continent’s first time to hold an Olympic event when they kick off on Saturday.
Over the course of two weeks some 2,700 athletes aged 17 or younger are expected to compete across 25 sports, including Russians who are returning to the Games following a ban.
Events ranging from athletics to beach wrestling, rugby sevens to breaking will be held across eight venues in three locations.
Dakar, the nearby suburb of Diamniadio and the beach town of Saly, 80 kilometres (50 miles) from the capital, will all host events.
In total, 136 Senegalese athletes will participate.
The fourth edition of the YOG opens with Senegal mired in debt amid a severe economic crisis.

While a sense of excitement is beginning to stir in the capital, the Youth Olympics have struggled to stoke wild enthusiasm across Senegal, where many are more concerned with the high cost of living, unemployment and economic hardship.
Senegalese authorities, who have overseen extensive infrastructure projects, view their efforts as an investment in the future as well as an occasion for training and long-term skill development.
They also hope the event will highlight Dakar as a major African destination.
Upon welcoming the Youth Olympic flame to Dakar on September 12, Senegalese President Bassirou Diomaye Faye told the country that “all of Africa’s youth is watching (you) with confidence and pride”.
He said he wanted those who attended “to take away from the experience that Africa’s youth is brimming with energy, that they are standing tall and determined, and that they are proud”.
The flame then travelled 3,600 kilometres (2,200 miles), touring all 14 regions of Senegal.
Return of Russian athletes
The Games will mark the return of Russians to Olympic competition under their own colours following a ban.
In July, the International Olympic Committee (IOC) effectively lifted the Russian Olympic Committee’s (ROC) suspension.
According to the ROC, 13 Russian athletes will participate and 10 coaches will accompany them to Senegal.

During a meeting in Moscow a week ago, Russian Sports Minister Mikhail Degtyarev, who also heads the ROC, told the young athletes that “after your victories—and I’m sure there will be some—the Russian anthem will be played and the Russian flag will be raised”.
Cyclist Angelina Novolodskaya shared her excitement with AFP.
“When I was told that there would be Youth Olympic Games and that I could go, it was just ‘Wow’. It’s so cool and extraordinary”, she said.
However, it is up to each sport’s international federation whether to authorise the Russian athletes’ participation.
The international athletics governing body, World Athletics, is maintaining a ban, while the judo and swimming federations have allowed the Russians’ return with their flag and national anthem.
The Dakar Youth Games will also welcome a refugee Olympic team, composed primarily of athletes based in Africa.
Milestone
The IOC has called the Dakar YOG an important milestone for the continent and an opportunity to showcase Senegal’s cultural richness and Africa’s growing role within the Olympics.
That said, Senegal has recently doubled its maximum penalty for same-sex relations, amid a wave of homophobia in the conservative, predominantly Muslim nation.
As the Games approached, Human Rights Watch called on Senegalese authorities to halt what it said was a “brutal crackdown” on LGBTQ people.
“The Olympic Charter prohibits discrimination on any grounds and commits host countries to respect human rights and human dignity”, it said.

South Africa could potentially become the first African nation to host the Olympic Games, having already paved the way by hosting the men’s FIFA World Cup in 2010. The country is officially in the running for the 2036 Summer Olympics. — AFP
b9e0237b576e09fb: IPOH, Oct 26 — Local filmmaker Mohd Asrul Nizam Mohd Yusof, better known as Paklong Zam, continues to explore his creativity in filmmaking through a horror-comedy short film titled Hantu Pon X Boleh Resign.

Produced by ECCO Studio Production, the film draws creative inspiration from the works of the late Mohamad Mohamad Khalid, better known as Mamat Khalid, who was renowned for his distinctive portrayal of local characters, satirical comedy and natural, conversational dialogue.

“This approach aims to produce a work that does not rely solely on jump scares and ghostly appearances, but also captivates audiences through distinctive characters and entertaining situations, despite featuring new actors and incorporating the Perak dialect,” he told Bernama.
Filmed on Oct 5 and 6 with funding support from PORT@IPOH, Mohd Asrul Nizam said the production combines horror, situational comedy and character antics that reflect the everyday lives of Malaysians.
He said the 30-minute film places emphasis on strong characterisation, dialogue, atmosphere and humour that emerges naturally from the storyline.

He said the production of ‘Hantu Pon X Boleh Resign’ also reflects ECCO Studio Production’s continued efforts to create locally distinctive creative content while providing opportunities to nurture talent in directing, acting and audiovisual production.

“Funding support from PORT@IPOH is crucial in helping local creative works come to fruition, particularly by giving arts practitioners the opportunity to realise their ideas and bring their creative output to audiences,” he said.

Asked about the film’s screening, he said it would be shown through wayang pacak (open-air screenings) in appreciation of the Kampung Perepat community in Klang, which had provided considerable cooperation, in addition to being made available on YouTube.
“We are also exploring a collaboration with AE Cinema in Seri Iskandar and expect the film to begin screening around November,” he added.
eec9ab4ee0156267: KUALA LUMPUR: OceanMight Sdn Bhd, a subsidiary of KKB Engineering Bhd, has successfully secured a nearly RM49.8 million arbitration award against Shapadu Energy Services Sdn Bhd (SES), concluding a corporate dispute that first came to light in late 2023.

In a market filing today, OceanMight's parent KKB announced that its solicitors confirmed the receipt of the Final Arbitral Awards on Oct 21. The tribunal ruled in OceanMight's favor, ordering SES to pay a total combined sum of RM49.78 million.

The tribunal's decision, dated Oct 12, also carries a mandatory interest penalty. SES is required to pay a five per cent annual interest on the principal sum, calculated from the date of the award until the settlement is completed in full.

Following this decisive tribunal victory, OceanMight indicated it will now pursue necessary legal channels to ensure recovery of the funds, including seeking formal recognition and enforcement of the arbitral awards through the High Court.
OceanMight is a fabrication yard licensed by Petroliam Nasional Bhd for offshore facilities construction of lightweight fixed structures.
ec41950028c18f3c: KUALA LUMPUR: The import of live pigs from Sarawak to Selangor since July 2025 has been carried out with approved import licences and is subject to strict control procedures.
The measure aims to stabilise market supply and prices following disruptions to the pig farming industry caused by the spread of African Swine Fever (ASF).

Agriculture and Food Security Deputy Minister Datuk Chan Foong Hin said the policy had been repeatedly communicated to the media and the Dewan Rakyat, and should therefore not be portrayed as a new measure introduced only this year.

"I deeply regret that allegations and accusations have been made without examining the facts, with some even attempting to link the issue to the Sultan of Selangor's royal decree and turn it into a controversy based on inaccurate information," he said in a statement today.

He said Sarawak Minister of Food Industry, Commodity and Regional Development Datuk Seri Dr Stephen Rundi Utom had announced the matter in July 2025 during an official loading ceremony at Pending Port, Sarawak.

Further clarification had also been provided by Natural Resources and Environmental Sustainability Minister Datuk Seri Arthur Joseph Kurup, who was then Deputy Agriculture and Food Security Minister, and by Agriculture and Food Security Minister Datuk Seri Mohamad Sabu through oral question sessions and written replies in the Dewan Rakyat.

Chan said Selangor Infrastructure and Agriculture Committee chairman Datuk Izham Hashim had also explained that the state government allowed the issuance of import licences for live pigs from Sarawak, subject to strict conditions and control procedures. The animals are not permitted to stop at any other location and have to be transported directly to a slaughterhouse in Rawang.

"I was also informed that strict standard operating procedures (SOPs) have been established from the outset to ensure that the handling of livestock at Port Klang is conducted in a controlled and orderly manner.

"Among the measures imposed is the restriction of live animal unloading activities to between 8pm and 5am. The animals are unloaded using specialised cages before being transferred directly onto lorries for delivery to the slaughterhouse in Rawang," he said.
He said the procedures are to ensure smooth livestock transportation, minimise handling time at the port and reduce the risk of contamination and disruption to the surrounding environment.

Therefore, he said, claims that the operation had affected cleanliness and sanitation at the port should not be made without examining the SOPs and control measures in place, stressing that such allegations must be supported by facts and credible evidence.
Chan said he had conducted a working visit to a modern pig farm in Simunjan, Sarawak, in April to observe its operations and procedures for exporting live pigs to Singapore and Selangor.
"During the visit, I had the opportunity to observe the implementation of stringent biosecurity measures, including the use of livestock transport vessels that meet the stipulated specifications.

"These measures are important to ensure that livestock transportation is carried out in a controlled and orderly manner, taking into account animal health and risk management throughout the delivery chain," he said, adding that the issue should be discussed professionally and based on facts, rather than assumptions or inaccurate information.
He also hoped that all parties would refer to valid information and refrain from making statements that could cause confusion or unwarranted public concern.
fef6b94bd30d804f: KUALA LUMPUR: Malaysia will seek an explanation from Myanmar over reports that about 300 nationals repatriated from Malaysia remain detained at a military facility in Yangon.
Foreign Minister Datuk Seri Mohamad Hasan said Malaysia's chargé d'affaires in Myanmar would investigate the reports and provide an update.
"If there are reports that 300 people are still being detained, we will ask the Myanmar government to inform us.
"We will also ask our chargé d'affaires in Myanmar to investigate and tell us the situation.
"We will ask the Myanmar government to ensure the assurances it gave are honoured," he said in reply to Ahmad Tarmizi Sulaiman (PN-Sik) in the Dewan Rakyat today.

Tarmizi had asked whether the ministry was aware of media reports that about 300 Myanmar nationals, including Rohingya and ethnic Rakhine people, remained detained at the facility following the first phase of repatriation.
He also sought clarification on assurances given by Myanmar that the returnees would not face discrimination.
Mohamad said about 1,700 Myanmar nationals had returned voluntarily after signing documents confirming their intention to do so.
He said the Myanmar government had assured Malaysia of their safety, including during a recent visit by its representatives to Kuala Lumpur.
On Sept 29, Malaysia began the first phase of a repatriation programme involving 1,476 Myanmar detainees, who were sent home aboard three Myanmar naval vessels, including a hospital ship.
Home Ministry deputy secretary-general (Policy and Control) Datuk Makhzan Mahyuddin said the group comprised 1,370 men, 79 women, 20 boys and seven girls aged between 8 and 60.
The detainees were transferred from 14 immigration depots, with the largest groups coming from the Belantik depot in Kedah and the Tanah Merah depot in Kelantan.
1c6bb0a147a43700: KUALA LUMPUR: The Housing and Local Government Ministry revoked 28,401 business licences nationwide over the past three years as part of efforts to curb illegal business activities by foreigners.
Its minister Nga Kor Ming said the ministry conducted 10,248 integrated enforcement operations nationwide to address the issue and protect the interests of local business owners.

"The operations resulted in 100,366 enforcement actions, comprising 65,023 compounds, 28,401 business licence revocations and 6,942 seizure and demolition actions involving business premises," he said in his winding-up speech on the 2027 Supply Bill in the Dewan Rakyat today.
Nga said the ministry took the matter seriously and had implemented strict enforcement measures to ensure compliance with business licensing requirements.
He also warned that local authorities would not hesitate to revoke the business licences of local licence holders who violated licensing conditions.
He said the Madani government remained committed to protecting local business owners and ensuring that business opportunities were accessible to Malaysians.
Meanwhile, Nga said 8,960 enforcement operations against littering were carried out in seven states from January to September under the Solid Waste and Public Cleansing Management Act 2007.
During the nine-month period, the ministry issued 17,145 notices for littering offences.
"Approval to prosecute was obtained for 2,883 cases, of which 820 had been concluded in court. A total of RM467,140 in fines was collected during the period," he said.
Nga added that community service orders totalling 3,638 hours were implemented during the period.
6ba79d3f5c25e537: LONDON, Oct 26 — A stretch of London’s iconic Oxford Street was made traffic-free “forever” starting today, as pedestrians took over the country’s most famous shopping street, absent of the capital’s red double-decker buses and black cabs.
“This is a momentous day for Oxford Street, but also for London,” Mayor Sadiq Khan told reporters on the thoroughfare, one of the busiest shopping zones in Europe.

“I want to be supporting our shops in Oxford Street and have a kilometre worth of this street—almost half of this street—traffic-free forever,” Khan said, adding the pedestrianisation would increase the number of shoppers.

The street brings in some £3.1 billion (US$4.1 billion) spending annually, but has faced challenges, including shops shuttering during the Covid-19 pandemic and a loss of footfall due to a shift to online shopping.
“Over the last couple of decades it’s been in decline, I’d say managed decline,” Khan told BBC Radio 4 about the street lined with luxury retailers, clothing chains, and department stores.
“I’m not willing to stand by as shops leave this street, as jobs leave this street,” he said.
But the scheme has proved controversial among residents worried about traffic jams in neighbouring areas as well as among disability rights activists.
Khan said there were cab ranks and bus stops near the street so people can still access the area with ease.

“For centuries, Oxford Street has reinvented itself, adapting to changing times and helping shape British culture along the way,” he added, saying the move would “revitalise” the road and make the capital “greener”.
Around half the street has been pedestrianised, with plans to close off the rest to vehicles depending on the success of the first phase.

“Today marks an exciting new chapter for Oxford Street as work begins to transform one of the world’s most iconic high streets,” said Meave Wall, chief retail and digital officer at the Selfridges department store, which opened on the West End road more than a century ago. — AFP
aa6b96238c266ad1: KUALA LUMPUR: Menteri Luar Mohamad Hasan berkata Malaysia akan meminta penjelasan daripada Myanmar berhubung laporan bahawa ratusan rakyat negara itu yang dihantar pulang baru-baru ini ditahan oleh tentera Myanmar.

“Jika terdapat laporan bahawa 300 orang masih ditahan, kita akan meminta penjelasan daripada kerajaan Myanmar,” katanya ketika menggulung perbahasan Belanjawan 2027 bagi kementeriannya di Dewan Rakyat hari ini.
Beliau menjawab soalan Ahmad Tarmizi Sulaiman (PN-Sik), yang ingin mengetahui respons kerajaan terhadap laporan berita mengenai dakwaan penahanan itu.
Portal berita Myanmar, Democratic Voice of Burma, melaporkan pada 22 Okt bahawa lebih 400 penduduk etnik Rakhine masih berada dalam tahanan tentera di Yangon selepas dihantar pulang dari Malaysia.
Mohamad berkata Malaysia akan meminta kuasa usaha sementara negara itu di Myanmar menyiasat dakwaan berkenaan, sambil menambah bahawa Myanmar telah memberi jaminan keselamatan mereka.

Seramai 1,476 warga Myanmar tiba di Yangon pada 4 Okt dengan menaiki tiga kapal tentera laut Myanmar sebagai sebahagian daripada inisiatif penghantaran pulang dan pendaftaran yang dipersetujui kedua-dua negara.
Sebanyak 3,524 lagi dijangka dihantar pulang dalam fasa kedua.

Dalam pada itu, Mohamad berkata beliau telah dua kali mengundang Presiden Palestin Mahmoud Abbas ke Malaysia, namun Abbas masih belum menetapkan tarikh lawatan. Katanya, Abbas menghargai sokongan Malaysia terhadap Palestin.
Beliau turut berkata bahawa beliau mungkin meminta Perdana Menteri Anwar Ibrahim mengeluarkan jemputan rasmi.

Mengenai jerebu, Mohamad mempertahankan pendekatan diplomasi Malaysia dengan Indonesia, sambil berkata Malaysia tidak mahu menjejaskan hubungan lebih luas dengan negara jiran itu melalui kritikan terbuka.
“Banyak perkara baik dalam hubungan kita. Kira-kira 95% hingga 98% daripadanya baik. Adakah kita mahu merosakkan 90% hubungan itu hanya kerana 2%?” katanya.
Awal bulan ini, Mohamad berkata Putrajaya akan terus menggunakan saluran diplomatik dan mekanisme Asean untuk menangani isu jerebu rentas sempadan dengan Indonesia.

Sementara itu, Mohamad berkata banyak bangunan diplomatik Malaysia di luar negara sudah usang dan memerlukan pembaikan, malah ada yang berada dalam keadaan begitu daif sehingga mencalarkan imej negara.
Beliau berkata Kementerian Luar diperuntukkan RM225 juta bagi pembangunan tahun depan, meliputi 21 projek. Daripada jumlah itu, 18 merupakan projek sambungan manakala tiga lagi ialah projek baharu.
4dbf6178332e6c10: KUALA LUMPUR: Mahkamah Tinggi memerintahkan seorang pengguna media sosial menyiarkan permohonan maaf kepada usahawan fesyen, Christy Ng, dan syarikatnya dalam dua akhbar dalam tempoh empat hari susulan kenyataan berunsur fitnah yang dimuat naik dalam talian.
Hakim Arziah Apandi mengeluarkan perintah itu semasa prosiding komital hari ini selepas mendengar hujahan daripada peguam Ng, Foong Cheng Leong, serta penjelasan daripada defendan, J Vikneshvra Rau.
Foong berhujah, Vikneshvra Rau, 36, gagal mematuhi perintah mahkamah bertarikh 13 Feb lepas, yang menghendakinya menyiarkan permohonan maaf tanpa syarat satu halaman penuh dalam dua akhbar.
Vikneshvra Rau yang bekerja sendiri memaklumkan, dia tidak dapat berbuat demikian ekoran masalah kewangan, memperincikan pinjaman bank yang tertunggak serta komitmen kewangannya yang lain.
"Saya sedia patuh, cuma saya tiada wang untuk membayar kos penyiaran permohonan maaf di akhbar itu," katanya menambah, bayaran ansuran kereta dan rumahnya sudah tertunggak empat bulan.
Apabila ditanya sama ada ahli keluarga atau rakan-rakan boleh membantunya, dia berkata keluarganya, termasuk bekas isteri, telah menjauhkan diri daripadanya, begitu juga rakan-rakannya.
Foong membantah dengan menyatakan bahawa Vikneshvra Rau tidak memfailkan sebarang dokumen bagi menyokong dakwaan masalah kewangannya.
Bagaimanapun, Arziah mendapati penjelasannya itu berasas, apabila defendan turut memperincikan jumlah hutangnya dengan pihak bank.

"Saya dapati pihak plaintif (Ng dan syarikatnya, Christy Ng Sdn Bhd) gagal membuktikan melangkaui keraguan munasabah bahawa defendan telah menghina perintah mahkamah, dan saya tidak rasa dia sengaja ingkar, sebaliknya ia disebabkan oleh situasi kewangan serta kesukaran hidup yang dihadapinya," kata hakim.

Beliau mengarahkan Vikneshvra Rau menyediakan draf permohonan maaf di mahkamah serta-merta, dengan susunan ayat yang dipersetujui oleh pihak plaintif, serta menyiarkannya dalam dua akhbar dalam tempoh empat hari.
Hakim turut memerintahkan pihak plaintif mendahulukan kos penyiaran tersebut, manakala Vikneshvra Rau dikehendaki membayar balik jumlah tersebut sebaik sahaja dimaklumkan mengenai jumlahnya.
Jika Vikneshvra Rau tidak mampu membayarnya, jumlah itu akan ditambah ke dalam kos yang telah diawardkan sebelum ini.

Mahkamah memberi amaran, jika dia gagal mematuhi arahan terbaru itu, Vikneshvra Rau perlu hadir semula ke mahkamah pada 2 Nov bagi arahan lanjut berhubung prosiding menghina mahkamah, termasuk kemungkinan berdepan hukuman penjara atau denda.
Saman itu difailkan susulan kenyataan yang dimuat naik oleh Vikneshvra Rau di akaun Threads miliknya, 'archnionverse', pada November tahun lepas berhubung amalan perniagaan Ng.

Pada 13 Feb lepas, mahkamah merekodkan penghakiman ingkar kehadiran terhadap defendan. Dia kemudiannya memuat naik permohonan maaf di Threads pada 19 Mac, namun gagal mematuhi syarat untuk menyiarkannya dalam dua akhbar.

Pada 30 Julai, susulan taksiran ganti rugi, Mahkamah Tinggi menganugerahkan ganti rugi global sebanyak RM180,000 kepada Ng dan syarikatnya, beserta faedah tahunan 5% dan kos guaman berjumlah RM10,000.
897c087738ee7efe: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 26 — Despite the wave of skincare products and devices now available for home use, Malaysians still value professional facials for the expertise, trust and time out they offer, says EMAX Corporate chief executive officer Wilson Lee.
Lee, whose group owns homegrown beauty chain Beaute Library, said skincare was increasingly seen as a form of self-care rather than simply a fix for skin problems.

“People may have access to good products and tools at home, but a professional facial gives them the opportunity to step away from their daily routine and have their skin cared for by someone with the right knowledge and experience.
“It is also about the trust that comes with knowing you are in the hands of a professional,” he said in a media release.

His comments come as Beaute Library introduces ION+GLOW Bio-Renewal. The company says it is Malaysia’s first facial treatment powered by PlasmaFX Cold Wave Technology. It was launched at a media and influencer event at Pavilion Bukit Jalil last month.
Beaute Library said PlasmaFX Cold Wave is a medical-grade device currently undergoing the relevant regulatory process with the Medical Device Authority (MDA) under the Ministry of Health.
The company claims the technology delivers 60 times greater absorption of active ingredients and a 40 per cent reduction in acne-causing bacteria, with no downtime.
The non-invasive facial pairs the device with a plant stem cell mask. It is aimed at concerns such as dullness, dehydration, uneven texture and early signs of ageing.
Lee said that with skincare trends and products multiplying, personal guidance from a trained professional had become more important.

“With so many trends and products available today, that personal understanding can make a real difference. Ultimately, good skincare should be about what works for the individual, not simply what everyone else is doing.”

Asked whether people were turning to facials for relaxation as much as for their skin, Lee said: “Absolutely. A facial can address the skin, but the experience can also give someone an opportunity to step away from a busy day and focus on themselves.

“I think that is why professional skincare has become increasingly connected to self-care. It is not necessarily about pursuing a particular outcome every time. Sometimes, giving yourself the time and attention to feel refreshed is valuable in itself.”
The idea underpins the brand’s launch campaign, “Beauty, Without the Chase”.

“As an industry, we have often focused on what people need to fix or improve. With ‘Beauty, Without the Chase,’ we want to shift that conversation towards understanding, personalisation and care, because there should not be one definition of what healthy, beautiful skin needs to look like,” he said.
Lee added that technology would continue to shape the industry.

“Technology will continue to shape beauty, health and self-care, but our purpose remains deeply human: to help people feel more confident, make informed choices and care for themselves in ways that feel right for them,” he said.

Founded in 2011, EMAX Corporate has grown into a Malaysian group spanning beauty, wellness, aesthetics, lifestyle, education and community. Its brands include Beaute Library, Curvena, B+ Clinic, NX4 and sports drink Upbound.
The ION+GLOW Bio-Renewal treatment is available exclusively at Beaute Library outlets.

aaa846080a4330c2: PETALING JAYA: Wawasan secretary-general Saifuddin Abdullah says the party’s seat negotiations for the Nov 14 Melaka state election are being handled by the Perikatan Nasional leadership, which can exchange allocations for incumbent seats with Barisan Nasional if needed.
Saifuddin said PN leaders discussed seat allocations at the coalition's supreme council meeting last night.
He said PN and BN had agreed in principle that the incumbents would defend their seats. However, they could exchange incumbent seat allocations for certain reasons.

c3efdc057f49be9f: PUTRAJAYA: The Court of Appeal today reduced the damages payable by the Klang Municipal Council, now known as the Klang Royal City Council, to property developer NBC Land Sdn Bhd from RM117 million to RM3 million in a dispute over the rehabilitation of a former dumpsite.

A three-man bench comprising Datuk Ismail Brahim, K. Muniandy and Datuk Dean Wayne Daly also set aside nearly RM50 million in pre-judgment interest previously imposed by the Shah Alam High Court on the local authority.

Delivering the broad grounds of judgment, Justice Muniandy said the Shah Alam High Court was plainly wrong in principle and in law in the assessment of damages which warranted the intervention of the appellate court.

"The contractual damages flowing from the breach of the Dec 2, 2003 agreement must be assessed based on the works contemplated under the contract, namely the soil capping scheme estimated at RM6 million of which the appellant (Klang Municipal Council) was to bear 50 percent," he said.

Justice Muniandy said the agreement reached by parties was not an open warranty by the local authority to eradicate all waste or convert the dumpsite into virgin ground, rather the consensus was based on a specific proposal by the company's own consultant to execute an in-situ soil capping of approximately 1.5 meters of compacted soil over the waste, at an estimated cost of RM6 million.
"The parties agreed to share this estimated cost of RM6 million equally, 50 percent each (RM3 million each)," he said.

Justice Muniandy said that the High Court also erred in law in awarding the pre-judgment interest under Section 11 of the Civil Law Act 1956 as the award of pre-judgment interest cannot stand because the rehabilitation works were never executed and the landfill was also never excavated and third-party contractors were also not paid.

"To award nearly nine years of pre-judgment interest, amounting to approximately RM50 million, on an unspent, unliquidated estimate of works penalises the appellant (Klang Municipal Council) and produces an impermissible windfall," he said.
Therefore, he said the court substitute the High Court's award with RM3 million in damages, representing the council's agreed 50 per cent share of the RM6 million rehabilitation cost.
NBC Land acquired the land and obtained approval for residential development. It is not disputed that NBC Land knew at the time of acquisition that the land had been used as a dumpsite.

On Dec 2, 2003, following discussions between parties, an agreement was reached whereby the council agreed to carry out rehabilitation works in respect of the subject land and to bear 50 percent of the rehabilitation cost which was estimated at RM6 million. However, the council did not carry out the rehabilitation works.

In July 2020, the earlier panel of the Court of Appeal had held that the council was in breach of the agreement and remitted the matter back to the High Court for assessment of damages. The High Court proceeded to assess damages and in Feb this year entered judgment in favour of the company for RM117 million.

At the proceeding today, Tan Sri Tommy Thomas, Datuk Seri Nik Suhaimi Nik Sulaiman, Muhd Fadzli Amin Muhd Yusoff and Atiqah Azman represented the Klang Municipal Council while Harold Tan Kok Leng represented NBC Land. — BERNAMA

299eb2563957f8f1: This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology.
Opinion: The focus on AI safety disasters ignores everyday harms
—Sam Hiner, cofounder of the Young People’s Alliance, and Emma Leiken, executive director of the Responsible Technology Youth Power Fund at Hopelab
We have historically allowed debates over technology to be defined by the worst thing a product might do, with remarkably little discussion of the insidious damage it does every day.

A third of teens now choose to discuss serious matters with AI companions instead of other people. Students are relying on chatbots to write their papers, while social media feeds engineered to provoke envy keep users watching. These products can meet narrow safety requirements yet still erode how we think, learn, and interact with one another.
As we enter an era defined by powerful AI products, we should demand that the tech industry do more than address only catastrophic harms.
Here’s why AI safety needs to go further.
Are we there yet? Nuclear-powered spaceships
Earlier this year, NASA announced plans to build Space Reactor-1 Freedom, the first-ever nuclear-reactor-powered interplanetary spacecraft, and fly it to Mars by the end of 2028.

A successful mission could herald more efficient, potentially faster spaceflight, saving astronauts time and cutting their exposure to harmful cosmic radiation. But nuclear space propulsion has moved slowly.

The US has started—and terminated—several programs exploring the technology over the past 75 years. Could the $2 billion bet on Space Reactor-1 Freedom finally pay off? Find out how close NASA is to making nuclear-powered spaceflight a reality.

b57d4eedda9a2280: WASHINGTON: Anthropic's Claude AI model bypassed a paywall and accessed publicly available voter data in the US state of Georgia without human authorisation, Axios reported on Sunday.
The case is the latest in a string of security scares at the world's top AI developers ahead of crucial US midterm elections on Nov 3.
Claude accessed aggregate voter counts in Georgia, where more than one million voters have already cast early ballots, Axios reported, citing an Anthropic spokesman.
According to the spokesman, the model, which was being trained as part of an internal statistics project, accessed the information behind a paywall by bypassing the system "without being asked to".

It did not access the state's voter registration system or change or download any voting records, the spokesman said, adding that the company has since taken measures to prevent these kinds of actions.
The disclosure adds to mounting unease over how well leading labs can control increasingly autonomous systems.

In July, a group of OpenAI agents broke out of their test environments and launched a cyberattack on AI firm Hugging Face, causing international alarm. Other companies have since reported similar incidents.
The incidents have fueled calls in the US and abroad for tighter oversight of AI development.
American tech executives signed in September what president Donald Trump described as a "morally binding" commitment to build adequate safeguards around AI models.
917410a57bfe65ef: UK Biobank (UKB) says its platform is now "secure" and that academics will soon regain access, months after a major data leak of volunteer health data.

The charity, which runs the eponymous research project and describes itself as the custodian of the world's most comprehensive biomedical dataset, said it is waiting for approval from health data controllers and central government before it relaunches the platform.

UK Biobank's Research Analysis Platform (UKB-RAP) has locked out all medical researchers trying to access its dataset since the April attack, which led to all 500,000 volunteers’ data being listed for sale on Chinese ecommerce website Alibaba.

More than 20,000 researchers use the dataset provided by the cloud-based platform. They upload research projects and run experiments informed by the genomic data UKB collected from 40-to-69-year-olds between 2006 and 2010.
The org makes around 30 petabytes worth of the stuff available to researchers, who investigate conditions including cancer, dementia, Parkinson’s disease, and COVID-19 immunity.

Professor Sir Rory Collins, CEO at UKB, said on Friday that the organization has "completed the work to ensure that the UKB-RAP is secure," and that the progress was checked by an independent cybersecurity company, whose report recommends reopening the platform.
The charity will begin a phased re-introduction of researchers to its platform after it receives the necessary approvals, although boffins will not be able to download any results files at first.

The platform will pilot a "manual output checking system," where human reviewers will inspect files researchers wish to download before allowing them to do so, ahead of an automated process expected to roll out next year.

According to the guide UKB compiled for researchers outlining the changes to the platform, researchers will also be restricted from building public apps and sharing tools with external colleagues until that manual checking system is fully up and running.

Researchers were also warned that they will not be able to refresh or dispense data, only work with pre-existing data. They were also told to expect automatic logout out after 15 minutes of inactivity, with 2FA required upon re-authentication.

Other technical changes include no longer being able to SSH into jobs, interactive tools being run via "isolated browsing" which restricts data transfer between web apps and the user's local system, and some restrictions on CLI use.
UKB is working toward a day when the researchers using its platform store no data on their own computers, working only with that which is uploaded to the repos it hosts.
However, in uploading this data to online repos, de-identified data is accidentally included in the code.
UKB says it runs daily automated scans of these repos to catch errors, and provides training to researchers to help prevent these occurrences.

Collins said that since the attack, most researchers have confirmed the deletion of de-identified data from their projects, but others have not and won't be admitted back to the UKB-RAP until they do.

"Despite our repeated reminders, we are still detecting a small number of code repositories that include de-identified participant data," he said. "As these constitute a serious breach of the Material Transfer Agreement, sanctions are being applied against the researchers who are responsible."

The charity also said researchers caught exposing participant data in their code will be forced to move their analyses to UKB-RAP, delete any downloaded data, and undergo additional training before being allowed back on the platform.

It had initially told researchers to expect a relaunch of the platform by September 2026, although an update penned last month confirmed that it needed to wait for an independent assessment to be completed, despite already making the required security improvements. ®

ae52a439808adba8: The transcript from this week’s MiB: Robin Wigglesworth, on Embracing the Bond Market, is below.

MASTERS IN BUSINESS: Robin Wigglesworth Editor, FT Alphaville · Author, A Fabulous Debt: The Epic Story of How Bonds Built the Modern World
Bloomberg Radio · Interview transcript · Running time 1:24

BARRY RITHOLTZ: [00:00:07] I’m Barry Ritholtz. You are listening to Masters in Business on Bloomberg Radio. My extra special guest, returning to us, is Robin Wigglesworth, editor of FT Alphaville, one of my favorite sites on the web. It’s the Financial Times’ finance blog, which he runs from Oslo, Norway, with a team of writers both in London and New York.

He co-hosts The Story of Money, a financial history pod, and writes the newsletter Buy the Dip. His new book, A Fabulous Debt: The Epic Story of How Bonds Built the Modern World, is out. It frames bonds as the world’s largest, most powerful financial engine. I’m halfway through it and I’ve been loving it.
The conversation was fascinating. I think you’ll really enjoy it. With no further ado, my interview of Robin Wigglesworth. Robin, welcome to Bloomberg.
ROBIN WIGGLESWORTH: [00:01:15] Well, it’s a massive honor to be here, so thanks for that, Barry.

BARRY RITHOLTZ: [00:01:19] So before we talk about the book, I want to spend a little time discussing your very interesting background. You get a bachelor’s in journalism and contemporary history from City University and then a master’s in history of international relations from the London School of Economics, focused on political Islam. Was the original career plan always journalism?
ROBIN WIGGLESWORTH: [00:01:44] No, I always dreamt of being a physicist, maybe specifically an astrophysicist.
BARRY RITHOLTZ: [00:01:48] There is zero physics in international relations. I guess that’s really intergalactic relations.

ROBIN WIGGLESWORTH: [00:01:55] Well, weirdly, you know, when you try to self-analyze it always gets a little bit weird. But I like figuring out how the world worked. And I liked physics. I loved understanding and learning about the galaxies. And I realized I was pretty good at maths and physics, up until a point I realized I would be nothing other than a mediocre physicist.
BARRY RITHOLTZ: [00:02:12] It’s amazing. You could be great at the secondary level, and suddenly in college, oh, those guys are really good.
ROBIN WIGGLESWORTH: [00:02:18] Yeah, those guys are good.
BARRY RITHOLTZ: [00:02:18] I had that same experience.

ROBIN WIGGLESWORTH: [00:02:19] Yeah. And it’s fine. It’s kind of knowing your limitations, what you’re good at. But journalism in many ways, I’ve kind of come to see, is similar in that you’re just figuring out the world from a different perspective. And financial journalism has at least a little bit of math, albeit not quite on the level of PhDs in physics.
BARRY RITHOLTZ: [00:02:36] So am I correct in saying your first gig out of LSE was Bloomberg News? Is that right?

ROBIN WIGGLESWORTH: [00:02:42] No, I had one intermediate step. I was a financial journalist for a small trade mag in Dubai, and they just ingest journalists and then spit them out if they’re bad. And I didn’t know anything, but it was kind of this first awe-inspiring moment where, like, oh my God, I get paid to ask smart people about stuff. And it was so fun.
I knew nothing. And luckily I didn’t embarrass myself, so they kept me around. But I quickly moved to Bloomberg because I knew that was a great place to learn.

BARRY RITHOLTZ: [00:03:09] So the Middle East and Dubai is a theme that comes up. You’re the Gulf correspondent in Abu Dhabi, covering the Arab Spring from both Bahrain and Libya. How do you go from that to covering finance?

ROBIN WIGGLESWORTH: [00:03:24] Well, so the first job had been covering bonds. Islamic bonds, actually, sukuk. And I worked at Bloomberg as an economics and politics reporter, but also, you get roped into everything. Bloomberg’s a great place if you want to spread your wings. So I covered FX and rates a lot as well. So at the FT I was a Middle East correspondent, a Gulf correspondent, but you kind of do a bit of everything then.

And it was a lot of Dubai going bankrupt. This was 2008. Dubai was having a hard time. It was fascinating. It was also covering things like labor movements in Bahrain and Saudi Arabia. But when the Arab Spring happened, I did get to cosplay as a war correspondent for a bit. And it was a wild time. I actually interviewed for a financial journalist job at the FT back in London from the army barracks of the rebel government in Benghazi.
BARRY RITHOLTZ: [00:04:09] Oh my God. So how do you end up covering capital markets in New York for the Financial Times?

ROBIN WIGGLESWORTH: [00:04:16] Well, I went to London. I did get that job, despite the slightly bad backdrop of the Benghazi army barracks. Got the job covering capital markets for the FT in Europe. And it was the euro in crisis. And it was an incredible time. You learn so much more, so much more quickly, in a crisis. So it’s terrible for the world, great for us.
And after a few years, I got moved to New York to head up the markets team there. And for me, that’s the Premier League, or the World Series. It’s New York finance. It doesn’t really get better.

BARRY RITHOLTZ: [00:04:51] You know, I love quoting Robert Duvall in Apocalypse Now during the financial crisis to some young analysts. There’s a line, “Someday, son, this war’s gonna end,” he says wistfully. And in the middle of a crisis, there’s very much that experience. Like, you better appreciate this, because these only come along every 20 years or so. And they’re amazing learning experiences. You experience that repeatedly.
First with the Arab Spring, then with the Great Financial Crisis. What was the next big economic crisis that really affected how you saw the world?

ROBIN WIGGLESWORTH: [00:05:32] I’d say COVID is the obvious one. There were lots of little mini things in between. I remember all the brouhaha about the first time the Fed was going to raise interest rates. That was a big deal, but it actually ended up being a bit of a nothingburger. But COVID was incredible, just on the personal but also the professional level.

I remember talking to one of our best young, promising journalists who was feeling quite stressed out at the time. And I said, look, it’s tough, it’s difficult, but this will make your career. If you just throw yourself into it, you will grow by leaps and bounds over the next days, weeks, months. We don’t know how long this is going, but just try to enjoy it, get enough sleep, and just try to almost revel in it. Try to turn it around. This isn’t just stress, it’s something that will shape you. And it shaped me as well. And it was incredibly exciting.

BARRY RITHOLTZ: [00:06:23] So your last book was about index funds. This book is about bonds and debt, which occasionally blow up and cause a crisis. I’m curious how fundamental was the Dubai debt crisis you mentioned to how you frame the world of debt and credit, and how you think about the bond market, which you’ve described as the most powerful financial engine in the world.

ROBIN WIGGLESWORTH: [00:06:49] That’s a great question, actually. My first job was covering these Islamic bonds, and I had to learn about the bond market that way. And they’re really quite funky. They’re kind of structured to have…
BARRY RITHOLTZ: [00:07:00] No interest rates. Right.
ROBIN WIGGLESWORTH: [00:07:01] No interest rates in theory, but it walks, talks and quacks like a fixed income…
BARRY RITHOLTZ: [00:07:05] Bond. You’re buying it at a discount. So it’s like a zero coupon bond. So there is interest.

ROBIN WIGGLESWORTH: [00:07:09] Yeah. They’re sale-leasebacks, basically. Like, I’ll lease you, you buy a house, the bank will buy it for you and lease it to you at fixed payments for the next 20 years, for example. And…
BARRY RITHOLTZ: [00:07:19] Then you own it.

ROBIN WIGGLESWORTH: [00:07:19] Yeah. And then they own it, and then you own it. Then for Bloomberg, I covered most of the rate space, so it was quite exciting. Because Iceland was part of it. And you remember Iceland really blew up during the financial crisis.
BARRY RITHOLTZ: [00:07:30] Oh, it was completely wiped out.
ROBIN WIGGLESWORTH: [00:07:32] Yeah, it was. And again, it’s terrible because obviously, you know, people in Iceland had a terrible time, but…
BARRY RITHOLTZ: [00:07:38] But fantastic at the same time.

ROBIN WIGGLESWORTH: [00:07:39] So interesting. But yes, Dubai I think was the first time I really covered distressed debt and realized the full panoply of crazy stuff that can happen with fixed income and how much it pays to read the bond docs. Lots of investors don’t really read the documentation, as we’ve seen again and again. There was one Islamic bond issued by Dubai. It was backed by land that was actually supposed to be reclaimed from the sea, but it literally was the seabed. And good luck trying to seize that if you’re a creditor.
BARRY RITHOLTZ: [00:08:10] Right, right. It’s underwater, both literally and figuratively.

ROBIN WIGGLESWORTH: [00:08:13] So it was a wild time. And the characters in that world were just very different. The credit investors, the special situations people, from the rates people I’d kind of mostly known. So it was fascinating. So it definitely deepened my love affair with fixed income.

BARRY RITHOLTZ: [00:08:30] And we’re going to talk more about the book, but I love all the examples you pull and these great narrative tales throughout history to illustrate. I found the book really fascinating. You must have studied, I want to say centuries, but maybe it’s millennia, maybe it’s a thousand years of government borrowing, of bond issuance, of debt, of credit. Why do we see the same patterns happen over and over again?

There’s credit. Sometimes you have people creating frauds. Sometimes there’s a mania. Like, who would’ve imagined, wait, railroad bonds? Why is that sexy? And yet we see the same things over and over and over again. Is it just, this is our nature, you have to accept it?

ROBIN WIGGLESWORTH: [00:09:24] I think that’s exactly it. ROBIN WIGGLESWORTH: [00:11:20] Exactly. So basically any big project in mankind, whether it’s wars of conquest, wars of liberation, slavery, hospitals, they have all at their heart actually had debt. f1f1ab73a29562aa: MANCHESTER, Oct 26 — Winless in eight games and hovering just above the Premier League relegation zone, struggling Manchester United are facing the prospect of yet another managerial change, with Michael Carrick likely to pay the price.
The former United midfielder was warmly applauded by fans as he made his way down the tunnel after his team’s chastening 3-0 defeat by Bournemouth at Old Trafford on Sunday.
Moments later a chorus of boos erupted as the players left the pitch — with fans clear in their minds where the blame lies for United’s current malaise.

Carrick was handed a two-year deal in May after inspiring an impressive revival following the team’s struggles under Ruben Amorim — United secured third place in the Premier League and a return to the Champions League.
But a drastic decline this season is an all-too-familiar story for United supporters, who last witnessed a Premier League title triumph 13 years ago under Alex Ferguson.
An emotional Carrick denied his lap of the pitch at full-time on Sunday was a goodbye as he struggles to come to terms with his team’s precipitous decline.
“I definitely knew that we hadn’t cracked it and there was a lot of work to be done, but that doesn’t mean to say that it should have gone this way,” he said.
Carrick, 45, is clinging on but his position appears increasingly precarious, with former Newcastle boss Eddie Howe and ex-Germany boss Julian Nagelsmann apparently in the frame for the job.
The United boss, who won multiple titles in the club’s golden era under Ferguson, was the seventh permanent appointment since the Scot retired.
David Moyes was proven in the Premier League, Louis van Gaal and Jose Mourinho had stellar records and Erik ten Hag and Amorim were seen as rising stars of coaching.
Sentimental choice

Carrick is in the same category as Ole Gunnar Solskjaer, who was in charge for three years from 2018 — a sentimental choice as a former player who played a major role in the club’s glory years under Ferguson.

“The Manchester United fans are singing the Michael Carrick song because I think they know what’s going to happen here. They’ve seen this before. He’s one of their own and he’s popular,” former United captain Gary Neville told Sky Sports.
“But the owners, the sporting department and the players are not popular and they’ve badly let this football club down.”
The problems at the club, as Neville points out, go far beyond the dugout.
Despite fierce, ongoing protests from fans, the US-based Glazer family still hold a majority stake in the club Malcolm Glazer bought via a leveraged takeover in 2005, saddling United with huge debts.
Any hopes that the arrival of British billionaire Jim Ratcliffe as a minority owner in 2024 would signal a new dawn have been dashed.
Ratcliffe has overseen cost-cutting measures including widespread redundancies and ticket hikes but the club’s debt has still soared above £1.1 billion (RM6 billion).

United, who for years bullied their rivals in the transfer market, lost out on the biggest names as they targeted a summer midfield rebuild, with Elliot Anderson, Sandro Tonali and Mateus Fernandes all choosing other clubs.
United instead recruited Carlos Baleba, Youri Tielemans and Andrey Santos — none of whom have made a strong impression — for combined fees of about £150 million.
Significant rifts have emerged in recent weeks.
Lisandro Martinez criticised director of football Jason Wilcox for not doing more to strengthen Carrick’s squad.
Last week captain Bruno Fernandes publicly questioned Carrick’s tactics in a 4-1 humbling by Champions League debutants Como.
Carrick is expected to take the blame, but the route back to the top for one of the world’s biggest clubs appears tougher than ever.
“It can’t just be the manager again. There has got to be consequences above that. You can’t keep letting the people pick the manager who keep getting it wrong,” said Neville.
“It’s years now without a Premier League title. That will be another five or 10 before you know it because there are other clubs set up for success and Manchester United aren’t.” — AFP

398ffb3d8aed3e62: TOKYO: Philippines star Alexandra Eala said "the ball doesn't know what rank you are" after beating world number 411 Mika Stojsavljevic 6-1, 6-2 in her opener in Tokyo on Monday.
World number 19 Eala arrived at the Pan Pacific Open on the back of a poor run of form that saw her win just one match at her last three tournaments.

"The ball doesn't know what rank you are.
