The British player gave her more problems in the second set, but Eala was never seriously troubled and took the match without ever having her service broken.
"It's a little faster than the court I played on last week," said Eala.
"It's indoor, comfortable weather, not very hot. I think I'm finding my groove."
Number five seed Elise Mertens of Belgium also progressed, beating Japan's Moyuka Uchijima 6-4, 6-2.

55b6991584b19c2a: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 26 — The import of live pigs from Sarawak to Selangor since July 2025 has been carried out with import licence approval and is subject to compliance with strict control procedures to help stabilise market supply and prices following disruptions to the pig farming industry caused by the spread of African Swine Fever (ASF).

“I was also informed that strict standard operating procedures (SOPs) have been established from the outset to ensure that the handling of livestock at Port Klang is conducted in a controlled and orderly manner.

Chan said he had conducted a working visit to a modern pig farm in Simunjan, Sarawak, in April to observe its operations and procedures for exporting live pigs to Singapore and Selangor.
“During the visit, I had the opportunity to observe the implementation of stringent biosecurity measures, including the use of livestock transport vessels that meet the stipulated specifications.

He also hoped that all parties would refer to valid information and refrain from making statements that could cause confusion or unwarranted public concern. — Bernama

dac2d048eb7700bd: QUETTA: Thousands of trucks remain stranded on both sides of the Iran-Pakistan border despite the resumption of limited overland trade between the two countries, southwest Pakistan business representatives told AFP on Monday.

Two other businessmen based in Balochistan confirmed their drivers had said only vehicles with documents prepared before Oct 16 were being allowed across the frontier.

Saudi Arabia and Turkey signed the so-called Mecca Joint Defence Agreement in August, committing the three countries to mutual defence in the event of any of them being attacked.

e4304ae775ad878f: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 26 — Southern Africa and Southeast Asia are expected to face the sharpest rise in drought, heat and power risks following the 2026-2027 El Niño, according to a report by BMI, a Fitch Solutions company.

It said the El Niño weather phenomenon is likely to raise drought risk to cropland most in Southern Africa, Central America, northern South America and South-east Asia, threatening maize, rice, sugar, palm oil and coffee output.

“In past El Niños, the share of cropland exposed to high-intensity drought rose by 11-12 percentage points on average across these regions, with Zambia, Zimbabwe, Central America’s Dry Corridor, the Philippines, Thailand, Guyana and Suriname among the hardest hit.

“In South-east Asia, drought puts rice, Thai sugar, Indonesian and Malaysian palm oil and Vietnamese robusta at risk, and the region faces the largest population impact, with around 90 million more people exposed to drought on average in past events,” it said in a statement today.
Meanwhile, BMI said El Niño poses the greatest drought risk to hydropower in Southern Africa, followed by Mexico and Central America, mirroring the pattern for agriculture.

“In previous El Niños, the share of hydropower capacity exposed to high-intensity drought rose by around 19 percentage points on average in Southern Africa, led by Zambia and Zimbabwe, and by around 12 points in Mexico and Central America.
“South-east Asia, the Caribbean and northern South America also face higher risk, with the Philippines, Thailand, Malaysia, the Dominican Republic, Venezuela and Colombia most exposed,” it said.

BMI said power shortages are most likely where hydropower dominates the electricity mix, with Zambia and Zimbabwe facing the highest risk of load-shedding, costly imports and pressure on utility finances this season.

“Mexico, Thailand, the Philippines, Malaysia, South Africa and Indonesia face large exposure increases but rely on hydropower for less than 20 per cent of generation, so impacts are more likely to show up as peak-power constraints than as system-wide shortages,” it said. — Bernama
fbae1044a5505aa0: PUTRAJAYA: Joint management bodies (JMBs) cannot stop property owners from entering their own condominium units over unpaid maintenance charges, the Court of Appeal has ruled.

A three-member bench chaired by Justice Alwi Abdul Wahab, with Justices Shahnaz Sulaiman and Ong Chee Kwan, unanimously allowed an appeal by SL Land Sdn Bhd and Foong Wei Ching against the JMB managing Sentral Bazar in Nilai, Negeri Sembilan.
The court set aside a High Court ruling that had upheld the JMB’s power to impose conditions on entry by defaulters under the Strata Management (Maintenance and Management) Regulations 2015.

Ong, who delivered the broad grounds, said the regulations specified the measures a JMB could take against defaulters, including deactivating access cards, requiring them to sign a register when seeking assistance to enter or leave the building, and suspending their use of common facilities and services.
However, these measures did not authorise a JMB to exclude an owner from his or her own property.
“The sanction it authorises is an inconvenience and a record. It presupposes entry. It does not authorise exclusion,” Ong said.
He said preventing an owner from entering his or her unit was a far more drastic measure than those specified in the regulations and interfered with the owner’s right to use and enjoy the property.
Ong said clear legal provisions would be needed to confer such a power, but none existed.
The judges declared unlawful the refusals to allow SL Land’s directors and authorised agents to enter their units on May 4 and June 20, 2023.
The court also ruled that requiring the company’s shareholders to be present or consent before entry was also not authorised by law.

The court granted an injunction preventing the JMB from blocking access, while preserving its powers under the regulations and reasonable, non-discriminatory security arrangements applicable to all proprietors.
It set aside the High Court’s RM30,000 costs order and awarded SL Land nominal damages, as the company had not proved any substantial loss.
The JMB was ordered to pay RM50,000 in costs for proceedings in both courts.
Ivanpal Singh Grewal, Harwinder Kaur and S Nisha appeared for SL Land and Foong while K Muralidharan and Ahmad Amir Mukhlis represented the JMB.
c3a0c00f45783a82: History is littered with the ruins of failed memory technologies. But former Intel CEO Pat Gelsinger believes an emerging memory tech developed by researchers at Georgia Tech using oxide semiconductors may be the exception to the rule.
"Essentially, we’ve had no major forms of innovation in memory for three decades – SRAM, DRAM, and Flash as the only memory types in broad deployment," Gelsinger told El Reg.

"Fundamentally, they are combining the best characteristics of DRAM, SRAM, and flash into a new device that is both dense like DRAM, fast like SRAM, and scalable like flash," Gelsinger said. This is exactly the value that Z2RAM brings, giving better density, speed and power."
This explains why investor Playground Global, where Gelsinger became a partner last year, is helping to bankroll Nagare's development efforts.
SRAM-like speed, DRAM-like density

Founded by Georgia Institute of Technology professors and researchers Suman Datta and Shimeng Yu, Nagare Labs is the culmination of years of research into next-generation memory technologies like ferroelectrics and resistive RAM.

The technology is being built on oxide semiconductors and is designed to be integrated directly onto compute logic using 3D hybrid bonding technologies. In this respect, Z2RAM will fill a similar role to AMD's 3D V-Cache SRAM stacking tech.
If you're familiar with CPUs requiring additional L3 cache, AMD uses advanced packaging to bond a 64MB SRAM tile either above or below its CPU chiplets, effectively tripling their SRAM capacity.

Z2RAM is similar in concept, but promises bit density upwards of 5x that of SRAM in its first incarnation. So if you were to look at a 64MB SRAM tile, Nagare's Z2RAM tiles would offer 320 MB of capacity in the same space, at bandwidth comparable to SRAM.

While that may not sound like a lot of capacity compared to HBM-heavy accelerators like Nvidia's Rubin with its 288 GB capacity, or AMD's MI455X with its 432 GB, Z2RAM presents a major improvement over SRAM-based accelerators like Nvidia's Groq LPUs.

Today, Nvidia's Groq 3 LPUs feature about 500 MB of SRAM per chip, necessitating thousands of accelerators in order to serve frontier LLMs at scale. Z2RAM could cut the number of chips required by 5x or more.

"With the explosion of AI demand, we’ve seen an extraordinary demand in memory as AI is a memory-limited workload. With that backdrop, there is extraordinary interest and now capital available for a breakthrough that solves the bandwidth and capacity challenges that AI is creating," Gelsinger told us.
Look Ma, no capacitors
Nagare achieves this density and bandwidth feat using memory cells based on transistors rather than capacitors.

"In terms of speed, it's going to rival SRAM, but in terms of functionality, it is more like a DRAM because of the storage mechanism," cofounder Datta told us. "DRAM is one transistor, one capacitor, one passive physical capacitor. Z2RAM is actually two transistors, but ... we are using the gate capacitance of the second transistor to store the charge."

Because that charge is stored in a transistor, reading it becomes non-destructive, which allows for better latency than you would get from DRAM. That's because when a DRAM cell is read from memory, its capacitor is drained. "After your reading is complete, you have to write back into the cell," he explained.
The fully transistor-based architecture isn't Z2RAM's only party trick because Nagare is pursuing a technology and process which will allow it to stack these cells vertically.

While that might sound a lot like HBM or LPDDR, Datta says it's actually more akin to how NAND is built up in layers, which in theory means that Z2RAM should be dramatically cheaper and easier to manufacture.
A long road ahead

With its first seed funding round behind it, Nagare now has $5 million to further the development of the tech. As semiconductor technologies go, this isn't a lot of money, but Datta is also the first to admit the startup's tech has barely left the lab.

"Where we are is literally lab prototypes," he said. The company is currently looking for an R&D fab partner to help it scale production beyond the university clean room, with the goal of sampling working Z2RAM memory tiles within the next four years and a goal of production shipments within the next decade.
Datta says the company is also open to working directly with chipmakers to integrate Z2RAM into their designs, similar to how AMD worked with TSMC on its 3D V-Cache tiles.
The company also faces challenges with regard to integration.

"There's no standard that we have right now to integrate this new memory with the accelerator," Yu said. "To unleash the benefits of this high capacity, high-speed memory, we have to use 3D bonding, and right now there's no standardization for that."
"AMD, of course, has the V-Cache, but it's a proprietary technology," he added.
In order for Z2RAM to see wide adoption without an open industry standard, Yu tells us that Nagare may have to design an interface itself, which is no small task.
There are also validation concerns. Nagare is working with oxide semiconductors, which Datta tells us benefit from better thermal and radiation performance, but are also prone to atomic vacancies.
Even "single electron effects or few electron effects can cause the threshold voltage of the transistors to move just a wee amount, and that will be enough to actually upset that cell," he explained.
Because of this, a lot of effort is going into maximizing the reliability of the Z2RAM memory cells.

"There have been so many memory startups and they didn't succeed," Datta said. "You might have the most amazing memory technology, but you can never penetrate the system because of the stringent standards."
However, Datta believes the landscape has changed. Changing dynamics and the emergence of new protocols have opened the door to being adventurous with memory again. ®

2a22f78b8940aa0a: MOSCOW: Russia said Monday that it would not slow down its offensive on Ukraine despite upcoming US-brokered talks on ending the conflict but that it could agree local "humanitarian" ceasefires.
The Kremlin said that it was open to short-term "humanitarian" ceasefires along the front line, ahead of a truce in the ravaged Russian-occupied city of Oleshky.
A ceasefire is to start in the southern Ukrainian city early Tuesday, brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump after months of reports that residents faced dire food, water and medicine shortages.
Asked whether Russia would consider more local truces, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters: "For humanitarian purposes, absolutely."
But Moscow vowed not to let up in the overall pace of the war, even as the sides prepare to restart stalled talks under US mediation next month.
"The decision to resume trilateral talks does not imply any restrictions on combat operations," Peskov said.
"Our armed forces continue to carry out massive strikes on Ukraine's military-industrial complex," he added.

Russia has intensified drone and missile attacks on Ukraine in recent weeks, hitting energy sites around major cities in what Kyiv says is a bid to plunge the country into cold and darkness throughout the winter.
Strikes last year left millions without heating or electricity with temperatures as low as -20C.
The two sides are to meet next month with US envoys to discuss ways to end Europe's worst conflict since World War II.
Several previous rounds have failed to move the sides closer to a deal. Russia demands more territory in eastern Ukraine and sweeping military and political restrictions on Kyiv.
Ukraine and its allies say the demands are tantamount to a capitulation that would leave the country exposed to a future Russian attack.

ecf175436a1de533: Apple's iPhone Duo scores higher than its foldable rivals for repairability, but don't let dust get into its delicate workings.

iFixit teardown crew put a spudger and screwdriver to Apple's flagship phone and reached a provisional verdict: its repairable, up to a point, and the batteries can be replaced. The inner display and hinge, though, look daunting.

The foldable inner screen is the Duo's party trick, yet reports suggest it isn't going smoothly for every owner. Some describe dead-pixel lines around the hinge, and others see horizontal lines on the right-hand side of the display.
iFixit's analysis point to the Duo's clever hinge as a possible culprit, rather than a straightforward broken cable.

"The damage we're seeing in photos isn't right where the display cable passes through the hinge, but slightly lower, at a point where several edges meet and change how the thin display is supported as it bends," iFixit said.
There's a center support bar which, the team speculates, might not be dropping far enough. The result is stress on the screen, near to where it reportedly breaks.
As for how that could happen, iFixit dropped the Duo into a bag of glowing powder, and opened and closed it a few times. "The hinge," they said, "started crunching."

To be clear, the Duo performed better than rival brands' foldables in terms of dust ingress, however, there was still enough in there to make the hinge crunch. Removing that flexible display to clean it isn't for the faint-hearted.

The trim around the screen wasn't much trouble, and the thin film behind the Duo's seemingly creaseless appearance peeled off fairly easily. Removing the inner screen itself, though, took heat and a pick, and was far from easy.

The outer screen was much easier to remove, and accessing the batteries (there are two) was relatively straightforward, we're told. The teardown team applied voltage, and the adhesive released the power packs. The cameras, logic boards, and other components were similarly simple to extract, although iFixit notes that five different screwdriver types were needed to finish the teardown.

Aside from the inner display and hinge, the Duo is relatively repairable. "Replacing them takes a lot of work," iFixit noted, "and the price could put owners off repairing the phone at all." With the kind of money the Duo demands, AppleCare+ coverage looks like a sensible safeguard, especially given the trickle of screen-failure reports.

"For a first attempt, Apple has done well," iFixit observed, having provisionally given the device five out of ten, its highest score yet for a foldable. Conventional phones, such as the latest Fairphone, have, however, scored far higher.
"You’d better baby that screen, Duo owners," concluded iFixit, "And maybe quit carrying around that pocket sand." ®

158cabe74a744338: LONDON, Oct 26 — Harry Kane is favourite to become England’s first Ballon d’Or winner in 25 years when the award is presented in London on Monday, but he faces stiff competition from La Liga pair Lamine Yamal and Kylian Mbappe.
Alexia Putellas is the clear frontrunner to win the women’s prize for a third time, with Aitana Bonmati’s three-year reign set to come to an end after an injury-hit spell.
The ceremony to decide the world’s best male and female footballers is being held in London for the first time — 70 years after England winger Stanley Matthews was presented with the inaugural award.
Bayern Munich and England forward Kane struck a remarkable 73 goals in 65 games for club and country last season, propelling the German giants to a league and cup double.
But semi-final exits in both the Champions League and at the World Cup in the United States mean a triumph for Kane at the London Palladium is far from certain.
“I’d love to be able to achieve something like that. It would be a massive milestone in my career,” said the 33-year-old former Tottenham forward.
“I think my wife would prefer to know and my family... it’s very stressful for everyone,” added the England captain.
Only four players from England have won the Ballon d’Or. Michael Owen was the last to triumph in 2001, following in the footsteps of Matthews, Bobby Charlton and Kevin Keegan.
Bayern coach Vincent Kompany praised Kane’s focus on his team, saying: “What made Harry happy the most in recent years is that he finally won his first team trophies here.
“Now if he can crown his career or his season with the Ballon d’Or, that would be deserved for the way he plays for the team.”
‘I deserve it’
Yamal finished second to Paris Saint-Germain’s Ousmane Dembele last year and the 19-year-old Barcelona superstar seems destined to be a Ballon d’Or winner one day.
However, a hamstring injury ended his club season early and he failed to show his most irresistable form during Spain’s World Cup triumph, which was built on impressive teamwork.
But that has not diminished his confidence ahead of the ceremony.
“For me, Mbappe and me, we’re the two best players in the world,” Yamal said last month.
“I honestly think that, as the best in the world, maybe there are two of us, and this year I would deserve it because of what I’ve won.”
Mbappe, by contrast, boasts plenty of personal milestones without medals for either Real Madrid or France.
The 27-year-old was top goalscorer in La Liga, the Champions League and the World Cup without winning any of those trophies.
His 10 World Cup goals in North America made him the top goalscorer in the competition’s history, on 22.

“Being the all-time top scorer in World Cup history, overtaking all the great legends in the history of the sport in the most important tournament there is, is something that really stands out,” said Mbappe.
“Who am I voting for? Myself.”
The Ballon d’Or was established by the magazine France Football, with the first award given to Matthews in 1956.
One football journalist from each of the 100 top nations in Fifa’s rankings is invited to cast votes for their top 10 players from a 30-man shortlist.
Although the award carries no cash prize, it can generate huge bonuses from clubs and commercial partners as well as increasing a player’s overall market value.
Putellas, winner of the women’s award in 2021 and 2022, was a member of the Barcelona side that regained the Champions League last season before moving to London City Lionesses.
Her former Barcelona team-mate, Poland’s Ewa Pajor, is Putellas’s main challenger after scoring 11 Champions League goals in Barca’s latest triumph. — AFP

4c574ac7e0e3957e: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 26 — Japanese seafood exports to Malaysia rose by about 40 per cent in the first eight months of 2026, driven by stronger demand for premium products and growing consumer appreciation of Japanese cuisine.

“Between January and August 2026, Japanese seafood exports to Malaysia increased by approximately 40 per cent to around five billion yen compared with the same period last year,” he said in his opening remarks at the Japanese Seafood B2B Trade Meeting Event here today.

To strengthen market access, Jetro will continue supporting Japanese small and medium enterprises by helping them participate in food-related exhibitions, business-matching programmes, and networking events that connect Japanese suppliers with Malaysian buyers.
Hirano said a weaker Japanese yen could improve the price competitiveness of Japanese food products overseas, although exchange rates are only one factor influencing purchasing decisions.

ffb649aab37e464e: PETALING JAYA: Countries investing heavily in data centres and critical mineral processing risk losing money if emerging technologies reduce demand for what they are building, Oxford economist Amir Lebdioui has warned.
Amir said governments should weigh the long-term risks before committing billions to industries that could change dramatically within a decade.
"I think it's quite unlikely that data centres in 10 years will look the same as today,” the Algerian national said in a podcast with Shahril Hamdan.
Amir said if a country hosts data centres, they are essentially at risk of building obsolete infrastructure.
He cited experimental 5D nano-structured glass technology, which he said could store 100 times more data by weight than advanced conventional hard drives.
He also pointed to research in synthetic DNA storage, including work by Microsoft, which could allow vast amounts of information to be stored in much smaller spaces.
Amir was also concerned if governments were sufficiently prepared for technological change.
"Governments often don't have access to information on potential technological disruptions that could completely disrupt their plans," he said.
Malaysia has seen a data centre investment boom driven largely by demand for artificial intelligence and cloud computing.
Amir also questioned the benefits of foreign-owned data centres and their role in supporting innovation in the countries hosting them.
“If the data centre is locally owned or if the plan is to use it for domestic data, this opens up possibilities," he said.
Minerals could lose their value
Amir raised similar concerns about critical minerals, warning that countries may spend years maturing processing industries only to find that the resources being used are no longer needed.
He said at least five types of batteries are currently being developed, some without lithium and others without cobalt.
“It would be crazy to assume the mineral you have will remain valuable because it's currently needed for technology.
"It takes years for you to build a manufacturing system around that critical mineral, add value, process it, but by the time you get there, that mineral is not needed anymore," he said.
He urged governments to establish technology foresight units to monitor emerging innovations instead, and assess whether alternatives could become commercially viable in the future.
"My advice is that policymakers should make decisions with calculated risk," he said.
This would help countries decide whether to process minerals locally, export them while demand remains strong, or develop manufacturing systems that could adapt to technological changes.
Amir warned that political pressure to develop downstream industries could cause governments to overlook the risks.
"Politically, it's very attractive to tell your constituents, I'm adding value to the country's natural resources even if it's extremely risky," he said.
He cited Chile's historical dependence on natural nitrate exports as an example of how technological advances could weaken demand for a valuable resource.
He also pointed to Indonesia's experience with nickel and bauxite, saying efforts to develop local processing industries had produced different results.
He argued that processing raw materials domestically was not always the best economic choice.
Governments needed to anticipate technological changes rather than assume that today's most valuable resources and infrastructure would continue to remain in demand, he said.

a27e75e428785fc8: LONDON: Part of London's Oxford Street, Britain's busiest shopping thoroughfare, went permanently traffic-free on Monday in an effort to revitalise the area and create a new public space to boost economic growth.

An almost 1-km (0.6-mile) section of Oxford Street between the Selfridges and IKEA stores is now closed to buses, cars, taxis, cycles, scooters and pedicabs, the office of London Mayor Sadiq Khan said.

The move has been more than two decades in the making. It and a wider regeneration project aim to put Oxford Street back among top global shopping destinations including New York's Times Square, Paris' Champs-Élysées and Barcelona's La Rambla.
"After so many false dawns, and now working with a government who share the scale of my ambition, I’m proud that we’re finally unlocking a new era for the street," Khan said.
"Revitalising Oxford Street will boost jobs and economic growth in the capital."

Oxford Street, connected to Bond Street and Regent Street and home to John Lewis, Marks & Spencer, Tiffany & Co and many others, has struggled since the COVID pandemic, with the arrival of US candy stores putting off many shoppers.
The pedestrianisation is the first stage of a transformation, although minimal construction will take place during the run-up to Christmas, a busy shopping period.
Plans for 2027 include more than 50 new trees, 100 new seats, two public squares, rest areas and better signage and lighting.

Oxford Street attracts around half a million visitors every day, according to the mayor's office, but many flagship stores including House of Fraser and Topshop have shut in recent years, and Khan said the area had been neglected.

"This marks an exciting new chapter for Oxford Street, creating a greener, more vibrant place that will attract visitors and investment, support businesses and jobs, and drive growth in the heart of our capital," British housing, communities and local government minister Angela Rayner said.

e2085c7b51d35b6d: LONDON, Oct 26 — British Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s new government unveils its first budget Wednesday, testing a commitment to ease the cost of living and ramp up defence spending with little financial room for manoeuvre.

It could prove to be a tall order for finance minister John Healey as rising inflation and borrowing costs — largely a consequence of the US-Iran war — increase the government’s debt pile and heap pressure on businesses and individuals.

“This is a budget that is about breathing space for people, for businesses too, and that helps bring a bit of hope,” Burnham, who replaced Keir Starmer as PM in July with their Labour party down in the polls, said Monday.
Speaking to the Good Morning Britain television programme, he added that the latest annual tax and spending plans will set out “the path to meet our Nato commitments” under a “funded” defence plan.
Labour had ruled out rises to income and capital gains tax, raising the prospect of spending cuts to balance the books, according to analysts.
The budget is expected to focus on smaller, more immediate measures to help ease pressure on household bills, they added.

“Priority has to be credibility first, which means a budget that clearly meets the fiscal rules, is fully costed and avoids large unfunded giveaways,” James Wood, professor of political economy at the University of Cambridge, told AFP.
“With government debt at around 94 per cent of GDP, the room to manoeuvre is limited,” he added.

Healey, whose official title is chancellor of the exchequer, has pledged to abide by the rules laid out by his predecessor Rachel Reeves, which state that day-to-day spending must balance with government tax receipts.
The International Monetary Fund recently forecast that Britain’s economy would grow faster than expected this year, before slowing slightly in 2027.
Banks to be hit?

0b20304fa1abe26b: PUTRAJAYA, Oct 26 — The Court of Appeal today reduced the damages payable by the Klang Municipal Council, now known as the Klang Royal City Council, to property developer NBC Land Sdn Bhd from RM117 million to RM3 million in a dispute over the rehabilitation of a former dumpsite.

A three-man bench comprising Datuk Ismail Brahim, K. Muniandy and Datuk Dean Wayne Daly also set aside nearly RM50 million in pre-judgment interest previously imposed by the Shah Alam High Court on the local authority.

Delivering the broad grounds of judgment, Justice Muniandy said the Shah Alam High Court was plainly wrong in principle and in law in the assessment of damages which warranted the intervention of the appellate court.

“The contractual damages flowing from the breach of the Dec 2, 2003 agreement must be assessed based on the works contemplated under the contract, namely the soil capping scheme estimated at RM6 million of which the appellant (Klang Municipal Council) was to bear 50 percent,” he said.

Justice Muniandy said the agreement reached by parties was not an open warranty by the local authority to eradicate all waste or convert the dumpsite into virgin ground, rather the consensus was based on a specific proposal by the company’s own consultant to execute an in-situ soil capping of approximately 1.5 meters of compacted soil over the waste, at an estimated cost of RM6 million.
“The parties agreed to share this estimated cost of RM6 million equally, 50 percent each (RM3 million each),” he said.

Justice Muniandy said that the High Court also erred in law in awarding the pre-judgment interest under Section 11 of the Civil Law Act 1956 as the award of pre-judgment interest cannot stand because the rehabilitation works were never executed and the landfill was also never excavated and third-party contractors were also not paid.

“To award nearly nine years of pre-judgment interest, amounting to approximately RM50 million, on an unspent, unliquidated estimate of works penalises the appellant (Klang Municipal Council) and produces an impermissible windfall,” he said.
Therefore, he said the court substitute the High Court’s award with RM3 million in damages, representing the council’s agreed 50 per cent share of the RM6 million rehabilitation cost.
NBC Land acquired the land and obtained approval for residential development. It is not disputed that NBC Land knew at the time of acquisition that the land had been used as a dumpsite.

On Dec 2, 2003, following discussions between parties, an agreement was reached whereby the council agreed to carry out rehabilitation works in respect of the subject land and to bear 50 percent of the rehabilitation cost which was estimated at RM6 million. However, the council did not carry out the rehabilitation works.

In July 2020, the earlier panel of the Court of Appeal had held that the council was in breach of the agreement and remitted the matter back to the High Court for assessment of damages. The High Court proceeded to assess damages and in Feb this year entered judgment in favour of the company for RM117 million.

At the proceeding today, Tan Sri Tommy Thomas, Datuk Seri Nik Suhaimi Nik Sulaiman, Muhd Fadzli Amin Muhd Yusoff and Atiqah Azman represented the Klang Municipal Council while Harold Tan Kok Leng represented NBC Land. — Bernama

cf452128dceeaf85: The UK government is throwing £130 million at AI-powered cyber defenses, including plans to deploy autonomous AI agents across critical infrastructure to hunt down security flaws before attackers get there first.

The money is part of a wider £600 million-plus AI spending spree announced by the Treasury ahead of this week's Budget, with ministers also promising to tackle biological threats, bankroll British AI firms, and reduce the country's dependence on foreign technology.

Of the cyber funding, £60 million will go towards a new National Cyber Shield that uses agentic AI to bolster Britain's defenses. That includes a £25 million challenge fund for UK cybersecurity firms and plans for a regulatory sandbox to test autonomous security tools across critical infrastructure, government and industry.
Another £70 million will establish the National Exposure and Real-Time Vulnerability (NERV) Centre, using AI to sniff out vulnerabilities across Britain's infrastructure and wider economy.
The announcement comes just days after the PHP2Shell security scare, which saw dozens of government websites taken offline after critical flaws were discovered in the widely used scripting language.

Britain's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) worked with OpenAI to coordinate disclosure of the PHP flaws and give affected vendors time to prepare fixes, after AI-assisted researchers uncovered the vulnerabilities.

Whitehall has already been experimenting with AI-powered vulnerability hunting. AI minister Kanishka Narayan said last week that the technology had uncovered 500 previously unknown security flaws across significant parts of the public sector.
It remains unclear how much freedom the new AI defenders will have to act without human intervention, or when they'll be deployed.

Ciaran Martin, former head of the NCSC, welcomed the investment, pointing to the week's events as evidence that Britain needs to get its cyber defenses in order. "We need to padlock our systems, and harness AI for defense," he said.
The Treasury is also handing another £120 million to the AI Security Institute (AISI), which tests advanced AI systems for dangerous capabilities and researches ways to keep them under control.

Cybersecurity isn't the only threat keeping ministers busy. Another £165 million will fund a National AI Biosecurity Initiative, including £100 million for what the government claims will be the world's first dedicated AI Biosecurity Lab.

The independent, non-profit lab will use frontier AI models to detect biological threats and accelerate the development of vaccines and treatments. OpenAI is contributing £100 million in compute and model credits, while Anthropic is offering up to £100 million in model credits, model access and technical support.
Google DeepMind and British biotech firm Basecamp Research are also involved, while the remaining £65 million will go towards biosurveillance and medical countermeasures against dangerous pathogens.

There's something for the homegrown AI industry, too. The government is adding £60 million to its Sovereign AI Fund to invest in British companies developing technologies including robotics and autonomous systems, plus another £60 million for AI research and development procurement.

A further £18 million will fund an Advanced Chip Design Academy, intended to help Britain develop more of its own semiconductor expertise rather than relying quite so heavily on technology designed overseas.

The package also includes £30 million for local AI partnerships, £15 million for an AI challenge prize initially focused on healthcare, and £23 million for research into AI's impact on jobs and the economy. Manchester will get a new NCSC AI Cyber Security Centre of Excellence to train government specialists.
Additionally, ministers are setting aside £10 million a year to study how AI will reshape employment and industry, including the jobs it might make redundant.
The government clearly has high hopes for AI. Whether the technology can live up to them without creating a fresh set of problems is another matter.®

51372a1262c12af1: European open source database service provider Aiven says it has saved 80 percent of its AI token costs internally by moving to open-weight models and is building a gateway to help devs swap models in and out as required.
The Finland-based company built its business on hosting and providing open-source databases as a service, and in the last couple of years has moved into machine learning.

Speaking to The Register, Ville Lehto, Aiven’s VP of strategy, said that when dealing with open source AI infrastructure, it's not trivial to make something that can run across the different clouds. However, in giving its developers access to LLMs, the company wanted to manage its own token costs and control its "own destiny when it comes to AI usage."

After a wave of debate around so-called token-maxxing, developers have generally become more interested in reducing their costs by using a mix of models, including cheaper Chinese alternatives to the Western frontier models, and open-weight models which come at a lower cost.

Open-weight models have publicly released learned parameters, principally their weights and biases, and can be run locally or hosted at lower cost than the frontier models from OpenAI and Anthropic. Examples include the Llama Family from Meta, Qwen Family from Alibaba Cloud, China’s DeepSeek, Mistral AI’s Medium 3.5 and Devstral and, Google's Gemma.

"When it comes to this token use, as we witnessed early on this year, there are a fraction of users that are absolutely heavy users, and when it comes to their spend, a lot of it could be saved by actually using open-weight models," Lehto said.
He said Aiven faced a choice to either have strict token budgets or try to find a more efficient way of using tokens.
Opting for the latter, it implemented an internal gateway to help developers work with open-weight models more easily, Lehto said.

"We wanted to make it as frictionless as possible. We can offer our employees different open-weight models, be it Western models or the ones from Asia, and take on the frontier models. We've been focusing on the heavy users, and with them we see roughly 80 percent decline in spend."
However, since the performance of open-weight and frontier models varies, it was also important to use other metrics, such as the cost per task, he said.

Aiven built its gateway around the open source framework called LiteLLM, which it hosted. It added new features such as budgeting, access management, and added other open-source components. It runs the models on rented GPUs and self-hosts the models as well.

Lehto said Aiven continued to use frontier models but only to help plan work. "When it comes to actually doing things, we use a lot of open-weight models. The majority of the work is actually done with open-weight, but the most critical bits of the work are planned with frontier models. That's how we see most success at the moment."
Aiven plans to offer the gateway as a service to customers to help them manage token costs by making it easier to swap open-weight models in and out of their workflows.
"Since our heritage is in open source, it's something that we feel very natural… offering as a service for people in the sense that it also fits the enterprise needs."

Aiven's customers include German ecommerce company Conrad, UK payment processing company Dojo, cyber security vendor Sophos, and communications firm Avaya. It is set to be just one of the vendors positioning themselves to try to help organizations reduce the costs when using AI. ®

2cfbf08c24101c5b: The technical details of web server stacks are worth learning about. Preferably not from the TV news. Last week, knowing about PHP was a niche professional interest. This week, cab drivers have opinions.

PHP is not the story; it's the illustration. There are good reasons that it has this most unfortunate of spotlights. It's very old, and it shows. Growing from roots in the mid-1990s, it has never suffered from the straitjacket of a specification, and while it has seen a lot of refactoring and modernization, it retains design elements from more than 20 years ago.

PHP is emphatically not the only project where urgent demands for better performance, reliability, and features consume the resources needed to tidy up ugly internals that appear to work just fine. Until, one day, that technical debt falls due. There will be many more days like this.

PHP's significance is that it isn't unique. The details don't matter that much, although this annotated comic book version is both fun and granular if you want to learn about it. Now the dynamics of AI-assisted cybersecurity are becoming clearer, defenders can use the tools to uncover dangerous flaws, but motivated and inventive attackers can use them too. Neither side has a monopoly on resources or ingenuity. The pace and scale of the conflict are growing so quickly that we have to look at how actual global warfare works to reconfigure.

The most pertinent aspect of PHP2Shell is the people, not the machines. We know how the LLMs identified the mix of problems and their exploitation over a few days in August, and we know how quickly any public information about such things can be weaponized. It took days, not months, to find, and hours rather than days to exploit. The correct protocol is to disclose patches privately to major, trusted organizations, and then when core services are protected, go public and go hard.

But PHP2Shell didn't work out like that, because it was too tasty a treat to keep secret. The first attacks were seen days before the anonymous Hacker News post that announced the presence and severity of the problems. That post had the correct CVE numbers. It came from someone in the loop.

The devastating effect of leaked intelligence and the tensions between keeping valuable data secret and being able to use it were abundantly apparent in the Second World War. This led to the system of clearances, classification, and trained liaison officers by which the output of places like Bletchley Park could be filtered, guided, and protected on its way to the people who needed it, and kept away from the eyeballs of those who didn't. It wasn't perfect, and security researchers don't need to work in huts while pretending to be supply clerks, but the lessons learned have proved good to this day.

Disclosure needs to be a discipline, not a protocol. It's no good telling an entire IT sec team ahead of time – the absolute minimum number of people should hold the secret for as long as possible. They have to be trained and trusted by the patch developers and their own organizations. If your organization can't field someone with the highest of standards, you'll go down the pecking order of when you're entrusted with the secrets.

Patch liaison has to become a hirable position with its place in career structures and qualification requirements. It needs to be part of an industry-wide structure where information can flow both ways.The presence and quality of the person in that role will define where you sit in the classified sequence of deployment. It's a way of managing risk in a very messy, very fast moving, and very consequential part of the IT machine. We need focus, intelligence, and skills just as much as we expect them elsewhere.

For all this to work, someone has to manage the whole thing across the industry. Tools and processes need to be developed with the explicit purpose of deploying without disclosure. Hand in hand with that must be a formalized system of identifying, analyzing, and setting in place expeditious factions for the most dangerous infrastructure components, both by deployed base and design nature.

There will be a lot of arguments whether PHP can and should be Rusted, for example, but no forum where the debate can be run to a high standard and appropriate resources provided to make the decision happen quickly. Expensive by some standards, staggeringly cheap by others.

We've never had to think formally about this as a discipline to be built to professional standards, but we've never had such a combination of complex, powerful attack vectors in a hostile and richly equipped environment. It's serious. It's war. ®

8b97b35d7a871fc5: Consider what passes for success in technology policy. An AI company promises that its chatbot will not encourage suicide. A social media platform makes it more difficult for children to buy fentanyl. These are important protections, and they should have existed all along. But companies can clear these low bars while continuing to make products that leave young people dependent on simulated friendships or trapped in feeds built to keep them scrolling.

We have historically allowed the debate over technology to be defined by the worst thing a product might do, with remarkably little discussion of the insidious damage it does every day. As we transition into an era defined by powerful AI products, we should demand that the tech industry do more than merely address catastrophic harms. We should take measures to ensure that its products don’t erode how we think, learn, and interact with one another.

A teenager who develops an unhealthy attachment to an AI companion may never appear in a lawsuit or a newspaper, except in the most egregious cases. Neither will the student who begins relying on a chatbot to write every paper, or the young person who measures their life against a social media feed engineered to provoke envy and keep them watching. A product can meet every narrow safety requirement and still leave our entire culture worse off in ways that don’t always make headlines.

A narrow definition of success defined around safety is politically convenient for the technology industry, and companies actively promote such definitions. Taking steps to prevent spectacular disasters is good for business: It can mean fewer lawsuits and less pressure for serious regulation. Confronting the everyday consequences of dependence would require something considerably more threatening to their bottom line. It might mean asking companies to add more friction to their products or actively limit engagement or features that lead to negative outcomes, such as addictive attention-hacking algorithms.

Technology giants have instead worked to shape legislation around the harms they are already under direct pressure to address. This year, for example, Google backed bills to regulate AI chatbots in several states. The legislation mandated basic protections against sexual content and promotion of self-harm that tech companies should have established regardless, but with broad carve-outs that could exempt some of the most popular services. Passing these bills allowed legislators to claim a safety win while efforts to promote stronger legislation—laws designed to prevent children from becoming emotionally dependent on AI—failed. This playbook worked in states like Nebraska, producing legislation heavily influenced by industry at the expense of bills that would have done more to hold companies accountable.

We have been through a version of this with social media. Globally, people who use the internet now spend an average of more than two hours a day on social media platforms—time that has been quietly taken from ordinary life and handed over to companies whose profits depend on keeping us there. No one, outside perhaps a few tech CEOs, wanted these algorithms to occupy such a large portion of our waking hours, and their cultural engineering can actually contribute to violence on a devastating scale. Meta’s platforms have been cited for contributing to the Rohingya genocide in Myanmar, anti-Muslim riots in Sri Lanka, and alleged calls for violence during Ethiopia’s Tigray war. The same incentives operate in the feeds that shape young Americans’ understanding of politics, their peers, and the wider world.

AI is extending this logic into parts of life that social media could influence only from a distance. It offers to write our thoughts for us and stand in for the people we might otherwise turn to. A third of teens now choose to discuss serious matters with AI companions instead of other people. MIT researchers found that young people using ChatGPT to write essays showed weaker brain connectivity during the task, and their evidence indicated that “cognitive debt” persisted even after the task was complete. There is plenty we still need to learn about the long-term effects. We already have reason to ask whether technology marketed as making us more capable is eroding the habits and relationships that help us develop capabilities in the first place.

Follow this way of thinking to its logical endpoint and you get a world of perfectly sanitized entertainment, with chatbots ready to spare us the difficulty of thinking or of dealing with another person’s feelings (or even our own). But anyone who has struggled to write something worth reading, or repair a damaged friendship, knows how much gets lost in that bargain. We build judgment through effort and friction, and we learn to live with other people by confronting the fact that they have needs and opinions of their own.

We should demand safety as a minimum, yes—and then demand considerably more. Technology companies and school districts should have to show beyond a reasonable doubt that AI improves learning and critical thinking before making it a fixture in classrooms. Companies should be prohibited from designing companions that pretend to be conscious or profess love to users, and they should face independent scrutiny of how their systems affect relationships and people’s ability to think for themselves. The companies that have inserted their products into nearly every part of modern life have earned obligations far greater than avoiding the next terrible headline.

Sam Hiner is the cofounder and executive director of the Young People’s Alliance, where he coordinated a coalition of advocates to pass laws regulating AI companions in eight states in 2026—laws such as California’s SB1119. Sam graduated from the University of North Carolina atChapel Hill in 2025 and was named to the 2026 Forbes 30 Under 30 Social Impact list.

Emma Leiken is executive director of the Responsible Technology Youth Power Fund at Hopelab, which has raised more than $9 million for youth-led tech accountability work, and teaches technology policy at the Columbia School of International and Public Affairs. She was previously TikTok’s global head of youth safety and well-being policy and worked on responsible technology at Omidyar Network.

"If you can be arbitrarily, at any moment, cut off from the American market, then it makes sense to have as much in your back pocket as you can," he told AFP.
"You look for something else, and that something else is Europe," Snyder said, adding that if the US trade war ultimately subsides, Canada will be in a stronger, more diversified position.
The EU, repeatedly ridiculed by Trump and his top domestic allies, is also looking for reliable partnerships in a world dominated by China and the US.
The bloc has let Canada into its defense procurement alliance and invited Carney and Canadian officials to attend key EU meetings.
The goal must now be to "move from writing each other love letters to real commitments," said Tobias Cremer, a German member of the European Parliament who has backed deeper EU-Canada cooperation.
Associate member?
The contours of the "associate member" status are not fully clear. EU treaties do not outline such a possibility.

A draft joint declaration that could emerge from the summit, seen by AFP, indicates Canada could join the Erasmus student mobility programme, the Galileo satellite navigation programme or sit on a proposed European security council, a conceptual idea backed by the EU chief.
Trump threatened to cut off EU trade after the bloc proposed associate member status to Canada, calling the idea both "laughable" and "a hostile act."
Trump isn't the only one to view the notion with scorn.
Angeline Furet, a member of the European Parliament from France's far-right National Rally party, argued the current free trade with Canada is "ruining our agriculture sector."
The Canada-EU Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement, signed in 2016, eliminates import duties on 98 percent of products but has not been fully implemented.
It's hugely unpopular among French livestock farmers and has not been implemented by several members of the bloc, including France.
The idea of closer EU ties has also riled conservatives in Canada, stirring accusations that ordinary Canadians will become subject to onerous European bureaucracy.
"We will never be the 51st state of the US, but we will also never be the 28th state of the EU," Conservative Party leader Pierre Poilievre said, connecting EU ties with Trump's annexation threats.
f4f84bb256f7090a: In all of West Africa, te voting age is 18, but presidential eligibility ages vary widely
Originally published on Global Voices
Youth mobilized in Africa. Screenshot from DW Africa's YouTube channel

In West Africa, young people can vote for the first time at 18. In some states, they are eligible to serve in parliament by age 25. However, depending on the country, they must wait until they are 35, 40, or even 50 years old before being eligible to run for the highest office. Although these age limits are beginning to shift, the real challenges often lie deeper in the electoral structure.

Young people are deemed mature enough to elect their leaders, yet not to replace them. They drive political movements forward by voting, advocating, campaigning, and protesting, yet cannot run for office themselves. The question is, can democracy really be called inclusive when it gives young people the right to elect but not to be elected?
Age: A shifting barrier

Across the region, the voting age is 18. However, presidential eligibility ages vary widely. In Gambia, it’s 30; in Senegal, Nigeria, and Côte d’Ivoire, it’s 35; and in Benin, Ghana, and Guinea, it’s 40. In the legislative assemblies, the bar is even lower. In Togo, Benin, Senegal, and Nigeria’s House of Representatives, it’s 25, while in Ghana it’s 21.

The situation in Togo requires closer inspection. On May 6, 2024, the country legally became a parliamentary republic. Under the 2024 Constitution, the eligibility age for President of the Republic is 50. Parliament also now elects the president, whose powers are limited. Authority now rests with the President of the Council of Ministers, who must be at least 40 and is not elected in public presidential elections. Faure Gnassingbé has held this position since May 3, 2025, the day parliament also elected the country’s oldest-ever incoming president of the Republic, Jean-Lucien Savi de Tové, 86.
However, the country’s legal age limit is hardly set in stone. In 2002, the National Assembly lowered it from 45 to 35 — a reform the opposition called tailor-made for Faure Gnassingbé.

More recently, in Ghana’s capital, Accra, on July 30, 2026, the Ghanaian government agreed in principle to lower the minimum presidential eligibility age from 40 to 35, defying the Constitutional Review Committee’s recommendation of 30. This legislation will ultimately go to a referendum, requiring a 40 percent turnout and a 75 percent approval.

In 2018, Nigeria set a regional precedent. Under pressure from the youth-led Not Too Young To Run campaign, the law lowered the presidential eligibility age from 40 to 35 and the House of Representatives’ eligibility age from 30 to 25.

According to data from the Inter-Parliamentary Union, lowering the minimum presidential age leads to younger parliaments. However, Côte d’Ivoire tells a very different story. In 2016, after removing the maximum age limit of 75 to run for office, incumbent President Alassane Ouattara, 83, ran for another term in 2025. The law rarely protects younger generations.
Youths particularly active in street movements

Even though young people have the right to vote across the continent, that does not mean all young people exercise that right. In August 2025, an Afrobarometer survey found that those aged 18 to 35 were less active than their elders in almost all traditional means of political participation. Overall across the continent, they trailed by 18 percentage points in voting, but by a record 29 points in Senegal. Protests were the only exception.

In Togo’s capital of Lomé, the June 6 Movement, sparked by the rapper Aamron’s arrest, brought thousands of people onto the streets. According to the Media Foundation for West Africa, the subsequent crackdown, for which the International Federation for Human Rights (FIDH) blamed government-backed militiamen, left seven dead.

Similarly, in Madagascar, the September 2025 protests toppled President Andry Rajoelina’s government, resulting in a military takeover. According to the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), the overthrown president himself came to power in 2019 on the back of a protest, at just 34 years old.

Comparably, in Kenya, street protests forced the withdrawal of the 2024 Finance Bill. Meanwhile, in Morocco, youth-led protests prompted the authorities to announce youth candidacy incentives and prosecute specific ringleaders.
Although leaderless movements wrest concessions, they rarely last without political parties or trade unions to sustain them.
The gap between participation and representation

The Inter-Parliamentary Report, published on April 9, 2026, found that elected officials aged 30 and under account for just 2.8 percent of all parliamentarians worldwide. Since 2023, progress has stalled for the first time since 2014. More than a third (37.1 percent) of legislative houses have no parliamentarians in this age group.

The lack of youth representation and participation is a significant challenge considering young people under 35 account for roughly 70 percent of West Africa’s population, according to the West Africa Youth Democracy Conference.

According to data from the Inter-Parliamentary Union (IPU), at the start of Ghana’s 2025 parliamentary term, despite the legal minimum age of 21, no parliamentarians were aged 30 or under. What’s more, those aged 31 to 40 held just 46 of the 269 parliamentary seats, or 17.1 percent. After Senegal’s 2024 legislative elections, the National Assembly had only five members under 30, accounting for just 3 percent. Although almost 38 percent of registered voters were aged 18 to 35, the Assembly’s average age was 47. Elected at just 44, the country’s youngest-ever president, Bassirou Diomaye Faye, only became an official candidate after his mentor, Ousmane Sonko, was disqualified.

In Nigeria, International IDEA, an intergovernmental organization that supports sustainable democracy worldwide, reported that in 2015, only three of the 360 members of the House of Representatives were between the ages of 18–25, rising to 14 in 2019 — a positive but modest development.
In Dakar, the head of Yiaga Africa, the organization behind the Not Too Young to Run campaign, summed up the situation, stating that the political arena is more open on paper than in reality.

However, Afrobarometer has identified a paradox. While young people do vote less than their elders, they are also excluded from seats of power and the polls. This representation gap is anything but passive; it breeds disengagement. The IPU warns that young people’s absence from parliamentary assemblies undermines institutional legitimacy and jeopardizes trust in democracy. Senegal, listed in the 2026 IPU report as one of the countries where parliament grew younger in the most recent elections, shows that rejuvenation is possible when a political agenda empowers a generation.
Rewriting the deal: money, parties, obstacles

High age limit proponents demand experience. Across the 34 countries that Afrobarometer surveyed, citizens favor an average leadership age of 39. Those calling for a lower age limit seek proven engagement measures, such as lowering the eligibility age, quotas, and forums for young parliamentarians. However, as Nigeria shows, often, the main obstacle is financial.

Nigeria’s ruling party, the All Progressives Congress (APC), has set the total cost of its 2027 presidential nomination and expression-of-interest forms at NGN 100 million (USD 75,000), NGN 30 million (USD 22,521) for the expression of interest, and NGN 70 million (USD 52,550) for the nomination. The Senate will cost NGN 20 million (USD 15,014) and the House of Representatives NGN 10 million (USD 7,507).

Young people will receive a 50 percent discount only on nomination fees, leaving the presidential bill at NGN 65 million (USD 48,789). A Nigerian civil society group calculated that workers earning the minimum wage, NGN 70,000 (USD 52) per month, would have to work for more than a century to buy some of these forms.

The Electoral Act, 2026, signed on February 18, also doubled the presidential candidate’s campaign spending limit to NGN 10 billion (USD 7.5 million) and tripled that of governorship candidates to NGN 3 billion (USD 2.2 million).

At the initiative of ECOWAS and the youth-led advocacy organization Legis360, delegates from 12 countries gathered in Dakar to bring these obstacles to the forefront. In their communiqué, they launched the West Africa Youth Observer Network (WAYON) and called for youth quotas, reduced candidate fees, and spending limits. ECOWAS later announced it would deploy youth-only election observers for Nigeria’s upcoming presidential election on January 16, 2027.

Other countries exemplify how laws can directly impact nominations. According to the IPU, Ecuador owes much of its progress to a 2022 law, which required 25 percent of its candidates to be young adults. Countries with term limits also have considerably more young parliamentarians than the global average. In 2023, the IPU also noted that limited youth funding and a lack of spending limits contributed to aging parliamentary assemblies.

Elsewhere, the obstacles are political. Take, for example, Benin. After disqualifying the main opposition candidate (Les Démocrates) for failing to meet election requirements, current President Romuald Wadagni faced only one opponent (Paul Hounkpe). On April 12, 2026, Wadagni subsequently won the presidential election with 94.27 percent of the vote. In 2024, a constitutional reform that extended the presidential term from five to seven years also raised the minimum vote threshold for securing seats in the National Assembly from 10 percent of parliamentary election votes to 20 percent. This regulation far outweighs a candidate’s date of birth when they have no party machine behind them.

Another example is Burkina Faso. In January 2026, the military junta dissolved all political parties. Meanwhile, in The Gambia, President Barrow will run for a third term in the December 5 presidential election.
Inclusive voting, but flawed representation

Is a system that gives young people the right to elect their leader but impedes their ability to become one themselves fully inclusive? The findings speak for themselves. Although Nigeria has lowered its age limits and Ghana has committed to doing the same, these limits are more a symptom than a cause. Age is not the sole contributing factor.

Critics argue that lowering age limits without also addressing nomination costs, party regulations, and the openness of the political arena would only be the first step on a seemingly endless staircase. What stands between young people and decision-making positions are exceedingly high costs, restrictive nomination practices, candidate exclusions, and even the lack of parties.

Until street movements have credible institutional representatives, they will continue to wrest temporary concessions or, as seen in Madagascar, give way to powers other than those they had hoped for. The primary challenge of the West African Democratic Pact is making young people not only the promised future of politics, but also an active part of today’s representation.
Written (Français) by Jean Sovon

b58cd02c6b98a218: TOKYO: Japanese companies are moving to pay compensation to users following waves of cyberattacks that have disrupted internet services and raised concerns about economic stability.

GMO Internet Group, a leading provider of online financial services, said customers would be compensated for losses stemming from unauthorised access following a cyberattack on its foreign exchange trading service, and all customers would receive ¥5,000 (US$32) as a gesture of goodwill, CEO Masatoshi Kumagai said in a blog post on Sunday.
"The internet itself is now starting to break down," said Kumagai, whose sprawling group includes internet infrastructure and cryptocurrency trading.

Japan said on Friday it would set up a team to simulate cyberattacks using AI to identify weaknesses in technology systems as organisations scrambled to curtail risks from flaws in the PHP programming language that underpins much of the internet.

More broadly, Japanese companies are being roiled by attacks with experts saying AI is helping automate tasks ​from scanning for software vulnerabilities to crafting phishing campaigns, making cybercrime faster, cheaper and harder to detect.
"The internet is increasingly being transformed into a tool that malicious actors use to threaten and rob people," said Kumagai.
Shares of GMO, which had a market value of US$2.6 billion as of Friday's close, slumped almost 16% to a four-month low against a 0.2% rise in Tokyo's benchmark index.

Government and company websites in Japan, Europe and elsewhere went offline last week after the disclosure of critical vulnerabilities in the PHP programming language prompted millions of hacking attempts.
Call on Japan to step up cyberdefence
Kumagai has urged the Japanese government to apply cyberdefence measures in response to the cyberattack, after the introduction of a cyberdefence system this month.
The system could involve steps such as attacking hostile servers to neutralise threats.
"Now is the time for the public and private sectors to work together to protect Japan," wrote Kumagai.
GMO said it received a demand for money from a party believed to be behind the attack, along with a threat to disclose company and customer information if it did not comply.
GMO said it would not comply with the demand and would respond to the incident in coordination with police and other authorities. It did not mention any connection to PHP flaws.

The company, which will provide a free alternative service to its customers for six months, said it could not currently calculate the impact on earnings from the goodwill payments and compensation for losses.
White-hat hackers working for the company had identified security issues but the depth and speed of the response were insufficient, Kumagai wrote.
Customer data protection weaknesses
The scale of recent cyberattacks has exposed weaknesses in Japanese companies' ability to protect their wealth of customer data and raised the prospect of surging costs to beef up defences.

"Companies already have standard security measures in place, so if they want to strengthen them further, there is a possibility that the additional cost burden could be quite substantial," said Shoichi Arisawa, an analyst at IwaiCosmo Securities.

The company said it would no longer retain identity document images after completing registration verification and expects to book an extraordinary loss of ¥5.5 billion due to responses to the attack and compensation payments.

62057dbdde85b043: BRUSSELS: The European Union will from Nov 1 slap a €2 (US$2.25) handling fee on packages from outside the 27-nation bloc in a bid to curb the influx from China.
The new levy -- coming just weeks before the Black Friday, Cyber Monday, and Christmas season shopping rushes -- will be on top of the EU's three-euro fee on small parcels.

The fee will apply to each type of item in a package sent directly to consumers from outside the EU regardless of the parcel's value. For example, if there are 10 T-shirts in a package, the handling fee will be €2.
But if a package contains two hats and 10 T-shirts, the fee will be €4.
The handling fee comes on top of the €3 duty imposed in July on small packages worth less than €150.
But European consumers will not pay the handling fee, insists the EU.
Online marketplaces including US platforms such as Amazon and Chinese retailers such as AliExpress and Temu, as well as sellers and other intermediaries must pay the new fee.
Platforms and sellers can, however, raise their prices, thereby passing off the higher costs to the consumer.
Why is the EU introducing the fee?
Nearly six billion small packages entered the EU last year, according to official data.
Some 93% of the cheap packages that arrived in Europe came from China, usually via popular Asian platforms such as AliExpress and Temu.
Brussels says this is putting increasing strain on customs authorities to manage this influx, thereby raising their costs too. The handling fee will compensate their efforts.
Since the EU imposed the €3 duty on small parcels in July, imports have fallen by around 64% -- although officials warn it is too early to draw firm conclusions.
Europe has also expressed concern about "unsafe" non-EU products such as toys that violate the rules arriving in the bloc via Chinese e-commerce platforms.
The €2 handling fee is a permanent levy but the three-euro duty on low-value packages is a temporary measure in place until July 1, 2028.
From that date onwards, standard, product-specific customs tariffs will apply.
The EU will have to assess the handling fee's amount every two years to ensure it remains proportional to the cost of customs operations in the bloc.

This week, meet a reader we’ll Regomize as "Robert," who told us he worked for an outfit that scours newspapers and websites to find stories mentioning their clients.

Six months later, another internal fan broke.

When the third internal fan died, management finally decided to buy a new box.
